speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will wish me to make a statement about the incident which took place over the week end in the Congo when Canadian soldiers were involved in fighting between United Nations forces and Congolese troops at Matadi, a port city on the Congo river some 160 miles southwest of Leopoldville, and the chief sea supply centre for United Nations operations in the Congo.
At about noon on Saturday, March 4, Leopoldville time, elements of the Conogolese army attacked a United Nations force stationed at Matadi. This force consisted of Sudanese infantry and a detachment of the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals which was operating the communications station for the United Nations command at that centre. The United Nations force returned the fire. The building in which the communications station was housed was hit by anti-tank, mortar and small arms fire.
Direct communications between the United Nations headquarters in Leopoldville and Matadi ceased at about 4.30 p.m. Saturday, Leopoldville time.
As soon as information of the attack was received in Ottawa on Sunday morning the Canadian permanent representative in New York, under my instructions, got in touch with the secretary general to try to establish the facts and to express the grave concern of the Canadian government about the fate of our men.
90205-6-169
I also instructed the Canadian consul general in Leopoldville to see President Kasa-vubu and the Congolese central authorities to express the anxiety and indignation of the Canadian government at the treatment of these and other Canadian personnel sent out to the Congo as part of the United Nations effort to restore stability and order. He was instructed to call upon them to do everything in their power to ensure the safety and protection of Canadian personnel. He was also to approach the representative of the secretary general in the Congo and the United Nations commander to obtain the release of our men.
Yesterday afternoon I received a report from our permanent representative in New York that a cease-fire had been arranged by the United Nations authorities with the Congolese at 11 a.m. local time on March 5. A period had been arranged for the exchange of prisoners and for the restoration of order, and for this purpose a mixed United Nations-Congolese commission was being set up. This report gave the names of the Canadians involved in the fighting as follows: Captain G. E. Belanger, Staff-Sergeant L. H. Harris, Sergeant F. B. Wood; Signalmen C. G. Bates, R. M. Beggs, C. B. Bostwick, G. A. Janules, D. J. Murphy and H. B. Strike.
In this initial report no Canadian casualties were listed but seven Sudanese troops were reported missing. It was stated that the secretary general had sent a protest direct to President Kasavubu about the Canadian and other detainees. Yesterday afternoon I received a further report from the Canadian permanent representative who had been informed by UN headquarters in New York that eight of the nine Canadians whose names I have given had been released and brought from Matadi to Leopoldville by United Nations plane. Three of our men were described as slightly wounded.
It was stated that Captain Belanger had not been included among those released by the Congolese forces to the United Nations. Captain Belanger had gone out to arrange a cease-fire at about four o'clock Congo time, March 4, and had not been seen thereafter. He was therefore listed as missing and action was taken to have his next of kin informed.
However, according to a report received half an hour ago, Captain Belanger has since arrived unhurt in Leopoldville. After the anxiety caused by the prolonged uncertainty
2668	HOUSE OF
Clash at Matadi in Congo about his fate, I am sure the house and Canadians everywhere will share my relief at this good news.
At this time I can only add that the Canadian government is deeply conscious of the indignation which must fill the hearts of all Canadians at the way in which Canadian troops have been treated by the Congolese forces. The Canadian government, through the United Nations Congo advisory committee in New York, is consulting with other governments which have forces under the United Nations command about the serious situation resulting from the apparent lack of control by Congolese authorities over their own troops, and about measures which can be taken to remedy the situation.
The United Nations is taking steps to build up the strength of its forces, and it is hoped that the presence of reinforcements will enable it to give increased support to its operations, especially in outlying areas.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I am sure all members of the house will have heard with both interest and relief the statement the minister has just made about the position of our Canadian troops with the United Nations forces in the Congo. There has, understandably, been created during the week end anxiety about that position in view of the reports which have come from the Congo; and while I think all Canadians realize that our members of this force have to face difficulties and dangers in an unprecedented operation of this kind, especially when facing troops of the local governments who seem to get out of control much too easily, nevertheless we all feel that whatever security can be given to them by the United Nations should be given. In particular, I think, anxiety was created by reports in the press to the effect that United Nations forces in defending themselves against the attacks were at times runing out of ammunition.
We can all join the minister in the tribute he has paid to our forces in the Congo, who have shown courage and discipline beyond all praise.

am sure all Canadians were concerned over the reports which were being received over the week end, and on that account we particularly appreciate the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Also, I might say, we congratulate him on his prompt inquiries into this situation which so greatly concerned the Canadian people.
I am sure everyone is relieved to know that all the personnel who were mentioned are now safe. I am certain it is correct to say that this incident highlights the fact that


Canadian troops and forces in the Congo are taking risks and making great sacrifices for a cause to which we are all devoted.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might say a word about this motion. On August 10, 1960, the Prime Minister reported to the house-his statement is to be found in Hansard at page 7943-on provisions for continuity of government in wartime. He said:
Provision must be made for suitable accommodation and essential communications. The functions to be carried on in an emergency must be determined now and individuals who will be concerned must be selected and trained.
The various federal departments involved in plans for continuity of government have been engaged in selecting the required key personnel. They would staff the central emergency facilities, together with personnel of the Canadian army. They would endeavour to meet those responsibilities arising in the emergencies of nuclear war.
It is not considered in the public interest that the names of those officials or their functions be publicized at this time. I am sure hon. members will appreciate that should this terrible emergency arise, it would be very unfortunate if enemies were able to take steps beforehand simply because of some information of this kind having been disclosed to the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 28 the hon. member for Laurier asked me the following supplementary question concerning water pollution:
My recollection is that the recommendations by the international joint commission to which the minister has referred applied to international waters. Have these recommendations approved by the two governments been implemented?
The answer is that the 1950 report of the international joint commission on the pollution of boundary waters and connecting channels was accepted by the governments of Canada and the United States. Canadian acceptance was given after consultation with the Ontario government.

We believe it is the responsibility of the province to implement the commission's recommendations. The government of the province of Ontario has taken an active interest in the matter and on March 28, 1956, legislation was passed in Ontario providing for the establishment of the Ontario water resources commission. This commission, which maintains liaison with the public health engineering division of the federal Department of National Health and Welfare, deals with sewage pollution in the great lakes and connecting channels.
Another supplementary question was asked by the hon. member for Lambton West, as follows:
Can the minister report to the house whether there has been any progress in the negotiations between the governments of Canada and the United States respecting the dumping of oil and sewage by ships using the great lakes system?
The answer to this question is as follows. The hon. member will recall that I have already referred to the regulations regarding the discharge of oil by ships operating in Canadian waters of the great lakes. To this I would add that the governments of Canada and the United States are aware of the problems associated with the disposal of waste, both from pleasure craft and from vessels employed in traffic on the great lakes and inland waters. Studies are being carried on by both governments to determine the suitability of existing methods of disposal. If suitable disposal methods are found, then consideration will be given to the possibility of drawing up the necessary regulations for implementation.

The house in committee on Bill No. S-2, to incorporate Aurora Pipe Line Company-Mr. Woolliams-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
90205-6-170
Private Bills
On section 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, this bill was intensively considered on second reading. Many statements have been made in regard to it. Some of the statements have been made almost on the assumption by the speakers that it was a government bill, when everybody in the house should know that, as a private bill, the government is not involved in it in the slightest degree.
The chief government whip made this quite clear when he interrupted the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam on February 13 and said, as is reported in Hansard, that the party whip was in no way involved in the decisions that are taken by hon. members in the private members' hour. There is no party whip on this bill. All members are entitled to speak on this bill as they think right and proper. When I spoke on second reading I said I would vote for the bill so it would go to committee, so that the questions which I wanted answered could be answered in that committee and we would obtain all the details on the bill.
The hon. member for Calgary South, speaking on second reading and asking the support of the house to give this bill second reading, said, as reported at page 1131 of Hansard, that if he was a member of the committee-
-I also intend to make a searching analysis once we have the witnesses before us.
He said further on the same page that after the committee submitted a report, this house would make a searching analysis of the report of that committee.
If I may refer to the minutes of the committee, I will deal first with the financial structure of this company. I would refer you, sir, to page 45 where, at the top of the page, the hon. members for Calgary South in directing a question to the witness spoke as follows:
You have already indicated to us certain basic principles of your financial structure. You have outlined the American participation and have made certain references in your opening paragraphs. You must have examined and given considerable thought as to why you wanted to proceed on the basis you have. Would you please elaborate on the details in your statement in regard to the necessity for this?
The hon. member continued as follows:
May I ask you one other question? Of course, you are aware of section 44 (d) of the national energy board-that in the final analysis, before a permit can be granted to you, the energy board must take into consideration the financial responsibility, financial structure, the method of financing, the extent to which Canadians should have an opportunity of participating, and so on. You are familiar with this section?
Before I go on to quote the reply given by Mr. Burgis I should like to return to the point

Private Bills
at which Mr. Burgis set out the basic principles of the financial structure of the company in question. It is to be found on the opening page of the report:
Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited was incorporated under the laws of Canada in 1926 and its shares are listed on the Toronto stock exchange. Approximately 10 per cent of its outstanding shares are owned by some 12,000 public shareholders, 22 per cent by the Hudson's Bay Company and 68 per cent by Continental Oil Company. Despite the disparity in shareholdings of Hudson's Bay Company and Continental Oil Company, each have by agreement equal voting rights and equal representation on the board of directors. The present board of directors consists of three Canadian directors representing the Hudson's Bay Company, three American directors representing Continental Oil Company, two Canadian directors representing the public shareholders and two senior officers of the company.
That is the basic financial structure of the company.
Now we come to the reply made by Mr. Burgis to the question asked him by the hon. member for Calgary South. He replied as follows:
Yes. We take the point of view that this is a relatively small line, and it would be quite usual for an oil company to build it as part of their normal operations. In terms of public financing, back in 1957 our directors did offer public participation in the ownership of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas, when there was no public clamour for ownership.
You say in 1957?
Yes.
But, what was the final result?

9.6 per cent-approximately 10 per cent-of the outstanding shares are owned by some 12,000 public shareholders.
It is not only what is said in evidence given before the committee; what is not said is also of importance. The question asked by the hon. member for Calagary South was quite clear in its intent. Although the witness answered in part, he did not give a complete answer, because a complete answer would have left an impression entirely different from the impression left by the answer as printed in the report of the committee proceedings. The proper answer is that prior to 1957 the ownership of the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company was 75 per cent with Continental Oil Company and 25 per cent with Hudson's Bay. The inference given here is that they offered shares to the public which were only taken up to the extent of some 9.6 per cent. Well, shares were not offered to the public. There were rights. I refer to the Financial Post survey of oils for 1958. On page 129, under the heading "Rights", that paper states:
Shareholders of Continental Oil Company and Hudson's Bay Company were given the right to subscribe to 1,744,592 company shares in September 1957-

This is what the witness was referring to.
-at the rate of one share for each 15 of Continental Oil held or one and one sixth shares for each 15 shares of Hudson's Bay Company held. Any shares not taken up under the rights offered were subscribed to by the parent companies.
Well, the shares offered were 10 per cent of the total number of shares in that company. Before this offering there were no shares of the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company on the public market and there were no shares held by any citizens of Canada or, indeed, by citizens of any other country as shares in that company. But after this offering, 10 per cent of the shares of the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company were available to those people who had shares in either Continental Oil or the Hudson's Bay Company, and because of the provision of one for 15 in one case and one and one sixth for 15 in the other case, all the shares were taken up except some 34,623 which were not subscribed to, mainly because they represented fractional rights.
Thus the implication in the minutes of the committee that there are two Canadian directors representing public shareholders is hardly sustained, and I ask hon. members to note that the witness is most careful to say "public shareholders" and not "Canadian shareholders". They represent those people who were formerly shareholders of Continental Oil and Gas and Hudson's Bay Company. When the witness says there was no public clamour for ownership the implication is that they were ahead of public thinking in this country, but this is just not so.
I suggest that with regard to offerings of shares in pipe line companies-and this is tied in with this particular pipe line company and the operations of its parent companies-the people of Canada are as prepared to put their money into risk enterprises as are the people of any other country in the world. In support of this contention I should like to quote from a clipping which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of April 29, 1960. This states:
Alberta Gas Trunk Line Company hasn't formally announced Its new $30 million preferred stock and debenture issue yet but local Investment men are already worried about how they will fill the anticipated demand ...
Investment dealers here say they expect to receive only small slices of the two $15 million issues and will be rationing the pie right from the start.
I would refer also to the financing of the Alberta Natural Gas Company a few months ago, when shares were oversubscribed two or threefold, and to the Trans Mountain Pipe Line Company whose shares, when made available to the public, were also oversubscribed three or fourfold. I suggest that at no

time has this company in question given the Canadian people the chance to participate in its operations even to the extent of one share, no matter what inference Mr. Burgis may have left with the committee. This does not strike me as being a searching examination of the operations of this company.
Now I should like to go on to another point which is referred to several times in the minutes of the committee. Section 44 of the National Energy Board Act, paragraph (d), is the pertinent part, and it states that as to financial responsibility the structure is designed to allow Canadians the opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and general construction of the line. I think I have dealt with this subject sufficiently by mentioning that in regard to the financial end the Canadian people will not be allowed to participate even to the extent of one share.
What is the situation in regard to the construction of the line? I feel I am being fair to the sponsor of this bill, as I have informed him of the information I have at hand. If I say something with which he disagrees he can correct me. I assume that he has been in touch with his principles. The information I have in regard to the construction of this line in Canada is that 41 miles is to be built by the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company, as well as the spur which goes across the border. There is only a half mile section to be built by Aurora Pipe Line Company. The contract for construction has been let to the R. H. Fulton Company of Lubbock, Texas. This was a negotiated contract and there was no chance whatsoever for any participation in this work by a Canadian company. When I conclude my remarks I hope the hon. gentleman will be able to correct me as to the accuracy of my information.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Could you reveal the source of the information which you are quoting now?

I have said that I received my information as the result of a telephone call to Calgary, and that is as far as I will go. I believe it is for the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill to put the facts before the house. He has not done so up to this time.

speechtext:
I would remind the hon. gentleman for Vancouver South that I have not found out as yet the purpose of his remarks at this stage of the procedure. I am attempting by my remarks to add certain information to the evidence given before the committee. I am adding information to the statements made in this house on second reading. Everything I have said pertains to the discussion on this bill. We have heard references made time after time to the effect that this company would be subject to the rules and regulations of the national energy board and the Alberta conservation board on oil and gas. The remarks I am making at this time have regard to the propriety of some of the statements made in the committee. I am elaborating on those statements in order to provide this house with certain information. I am very happy to be able to give this information at this time, because I feel that it should be brought to the attention of this house. It has been said that there would be a searching examination conducted in respect of the operations of the company, and I feel that that examination did not go far enough.
There were questions asked of the witness as to why Bill No. S-2, which we are discussing, carries a capitalization of $10 million when the Aurora Pipe Line Company intends to build only one half mile of this line at a cost of $15,000. The hon. member for Victoria also asked at that time if the construction of the one half mile section was all that company intended to do. It was brought to the attention of the committee that a latter part of the bill contained a request for permission to build pipe lines within Canada in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia and in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. Evidence was given that eventually the line might be extended into these areas, but at this time the company wished to secure the privilege of doing so in order to obviate the necessity of coming back to parliament at a later date.
Would the hon. member read the pertinent section?

I will read Mr. Burgis' answer, if that is what the hon. member desires. His answer is reported as follows:
At the moment, sir, we have nothing else specifically in mind. However, we are, as are many of the other oil companies, in the pipe line business. Frequently, when we consider moving crude or condensate from one field or one market to another it might involve consideration of crossing interprovincial boundaries and at that time we conceivably could use Aurora to build more facilities, let us say, from the Yukon or Northwest Territories into Alberta or something like that.
I think I have read enough of the answer to give the sense of the situation.

Private Bills
I was referring to the portion where Mr. Burgis went on to say that it is customary to include such a clause in the bill.

I agree that it is the customary thing to do. I am not referring to those subjects which come within the purview of the Alberta natural gas and oil conservation board. I am not trying to show that this line is economically sound, whether the reserves are sufficient, or to discuss any other item in this regard. I am now referring only to the basic foundation of this pipe line and how its application fits into our concept of ownership, control, construction and those items which are covered in the regulations of the national energy board, as well as the concept of the fundamental principles of this party and, I believe, of this government.
If this pipe line company intends to build only one half mile of line and then intends to make a connection with a line in another province I suggest the total expenditure would only be in the neighbourhood of $100,000. I suggest that the connection between Alberta and Saskatchewan would run only to $15,000; the connection between Saskatchewan and Manitoba, $15,000; the connection between Manitoba and Ontario, $15,000; and the connection between the Northwest Territories and Alberta would be in the neighbourhood of $15,000 each. Using this same reasoning, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited would be a company involving only $50,000.
In view of what I have said, I have asked myself why the Aurora Pipe Line Company is not in a position to build the 41 miles which will be built by the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company, and why they intend only to build the one half mile section. I have come to the conclusion that this is simply a device to allow freedom of action, away from the control of the national energy board, for a major section of pipe line. What this bill in effect says is that the company is going to spend $15,000 but will capitalize itself at $10 million in order to have some spare capital. This does not add up, in my estimation.
When we think of the discussion which took place in this house on second reading of the bill it is simply fantastic to me that from the very start the standing committee did not take minutes of its proceedings, particularly when we recall the criticism which was levelled at the committee in the other place. The committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines commenced its sitting at 10.30 a.m., and for 50 minutes the session proceeded without a shorthand reporter being present. At 11.20 a.m. the committee recessed when the hon. member for Yukon made a motion that the committee should 
recess until a shorthand reporter was available. The committee resumed its sitting at 11.30 a.m. and adjourned at 12.25 p.m., 55 minutes later. The committee tried to pick up the statements which had been made, but so far as the minutes of proceedings are con-erned half of the work of the committee is a blank.
That is not true.
It is not on record. I should like to say at this time-

On a point of order, I think the hon. member has certainly left this committee under a false impression. At the beginning of the committee meeting Mr. Burgis read a statement, which took somewhere between 15 and 30 minutes, and that is all reported in the evidence that the hon. member has on his desk. It is true that about 15 minutes of the proceedings of the standing committee are not recorded in written evidence, but that is about all, and certainly not over half an hour.
That is not true.
The evidence is there.

I did say the committee tried to pick up the lost ground, but Mr. Burgis' evidence takes up a page and a half. If it took 15 minutes to read a page and a half of evidence, then Mr. Burgis must have been reading awfully slowly. The point I should like to make is that right from the start I myself requested the committee to take evidence. I do not want to labour the point, but I did so because I was interested in the bill and I wanted to know what was said in committee. When this bill was before the other place there appeared as witnesses-
Did the hon. member say he sent a letter to the chairman of the committee which was not read?
No, I did not say that. I said that I advised the chairman and I advised the committee that I thought a record of the proceedings should be kept.
When?
I simply advised the committee that I thought minutes of the proceedings should be kept.
When?
Who wants to know the answer to that?
I do.
I should like to know the answer to that.
Does the hon. member happen to have the letter that he sent to the chairman of the committee, and would he read it to this house?

Mr. Chairman, all I wish to say is that I asked the committee to keep minutes of the proceedings. When this bill was before the other place the same witnesses appeared there, but at that time there was also in opposition Mr. James Scott, president of the Pembina Pipe Line Company, and in attendance but not heard were Messrs. Charles Crawford and A. Douglas Armour.
It is the responsibility of anybody who wishes to oppose a bill to make his wishes known to the chief clerk of committees, and then a meeting will be held so that those who oppose a bill may be in attendance. I wish to point out, however, that second reading of this bill took place on February 13 and the committee held its meeting on Tuesday, February 21.
I hold no brief for the Pembina group; I am not saying that this particular pipe line will or will not hurt them. I am not going to say whether, as between these two as operating companies, we should make a decision; but I do say that, on the point I am trying to make with regard to Canadian participation in financing, engineering, construction and the whole works, the Pembina people seem to me to have a much better record than the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company for the reasons I have already outlined.
In the committee meeting many hon. members and the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Bow River, pointed out that this bill simply gives the company the right to incorporate, and that members of parliament in effect are exceeding their duty when they check into this in any great detail; that it is really none of their concern. At page 30 of the committee proceedings the hon. member for Calgary South, in questioning the hon. member for York North, who appeared before the committee, made the point that the hon. member for York North was not qualified to pass judgment on the technical aspects of this bill.
And he admitted he was not.

At page 44 the hon. member for Winnipeg South made this statement:
I was just going to say that if they were strenuously objecting, they would be represented here by counsel. However, I think they realize this is a mere technical execution of a function of parliament and, undoubtedly, in the course of time they will appear before the energy board, if they feel disposed to do so.
Private Bills
It will be a sad day, Mr. Chairman, when we start to think of the operations of committees of this house and of the house itself as merely technical executions of a function of parliament. I say that every member has a right to ask questions on any bill, private or public, that comes before this house or before any committee of this house and try to ascertain the truth of the matter-
That is irrelevant.

-and that is what I have been trying to do. In regard to the operation of the committee itself, I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to citation 491(1) of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, which discusses voting in committee, and which reads:
The names of the members attending each committee are entered by the committee clerk in the minutes; and when a division takes place, the clerk takes down the names of the members, distinguishing on which side of the question they respectively vote; and such lists are to be given in, with the report, to the house.
These minutes of the committee appear to me to be the report to the house, but the direction as laid down in this citation was not followed. There was a vote in committee; it was a vote in which the hon. member for-

speechtext: Order. I must inform the hon. member that his time has expired.
Go ahead.
Let him proceed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee giving its consent to the hon. member proceeding further?
Yes.
Agreed.

I wish to thank the committee for its courtesy, and I shall try not to trespass on the patience of hon. members any longer than necessary. As I said, Mr. Chairman, there was a motion in the committee moved by the hon. member for Westmorland and seconded by the hon. member for York East. The intent of the motion was to defer clause by clause consideration of Bill No. S-2 for a period of at least one week in order to give interested parties the privilege of appearing before the committee at the adjourned meeting. The said motion was negatived on the following division: Yeas, 5; nays, 8, or a total of 13 votes cast.
Two of the members who voted on the motion in the committee have an interest in the bill. I do not mean that they have a financial interest or anything of that sort; they have an interest in the bill because

Private Bills
they have been sponsors of it. First of all, the hon. member for Winnipeg South sponsored the bill in place of the hon. member for Bow River; then later the hon. member for Bow River came back into the picture. Section 2 of citation 292 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms reads as follows:
A member has been substituted for another on a committee of the Canadian Commons on account of the member originally appointed having acted as counsel for the parties interested in the matter before the committee.
I do not know whether a sponsor is in the position of acting as counsel, but when you have a very close vote of eight to five and two out of the eight are interested because of their sponsorship of the bill, the margin is very narrow. There is also the point that for the first time that I can recall the quorum of this committee is 10 members. According to the standing orders of the house the quorum of a committee of 60 members is 20. As all hon. members know, the quorum is then reduced to a more reasonable figure, usually to 15 members. This time the quorum was reduced to 10 members. This has nothing to do with the bill, except that a very limited number of members have made a decision with regard to whether time should be given for parties who may be opposed to the bill to appear before the committee and express their objections in the same way they did before the committee of the other place.
In no case, Mr. Chairman, am I supporting the viewpoint of the C.C.F. with regard to the economic feasibility of the line. I am simply talking about the matter of Canadian participation in financing, in construction and in the operation of the line. In this respect it seems to me that the Pembina group who opposed the bill in the other place-and I have no interest in that group-is operating more in keeping with the National Energy Board Act and with what that act says a pipe line company shall do than is the case with the company that is now before us.
I think I have pointed out that answers have not been full and complete. In my opinion it is ludicrous that we should have all this talk about a $15,000 project. It is nothing of the kind. As the sponsors and the people behind the bill know, they are asking for a capitalization of $10 million, yet what they are going to do is build a $15,000 pipe line.
It is too bad that this matter was not investigated more thoroughly in the committee. It is too bad that when the proposed Pembina pipe line construction is to cost $40 million, as I understand from the letter filed by the hon. member for Vancouver East, these people should talk about a $15,000 pipe line. In

sponsoring the bill the hon. member for Bow River made this statement on February 13, as found on page 1979 of Hansard:
I should like now to refer to this red herring, as I call it, which relates to our position in so far as United States capital and United States companies operating in Canada are concerned. My answer to that is briefly this. I have never considered any words used by any members of the cabinet or any members of the government as being against capital coming from anywhere, whether it was from the United States or any country in Europe.
No one will disagree with that statement. That is true. We welcome foreign capital in this country. However, the hon. member went on to say something really pertinent with regard to such capital. He said:
The only thing for which this government has stood, and I am proud to be a Conservative in that regard, is that Canadians can compete on equal terms with capital coming into this country from other sources.
If the hon. member would change the word "compete" to "participate" so that the statement would read that Canadians can participate on equal terms with capital coming into this country from other sources I would be 100 per cent in agreement with him. What I have tried to do is to show that that right is not being given to Canadians under the proposed incorporation of this company, and no matter what the witness said it has not been given in the past. I think the bill deserves a much more searching examination in committee of the whole house than it received in the standing committee. I want to say right now that when the bill comes to a vote I will vote against it.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard an exposition with regard to Canadian participation in the development of our resources in western Canada. The bill now before us concerns me particularly, because in my constituency in Alberta probably more oil and gas are produced than in any other constituency in western Canada. As a matter of fact the technical people who are opposing the incorporation of the Aurora Pipe Line Company, the so-called Pembina group, have their headquarters in my constituency and are now operating Pembina Pipe Line Company in that area. However, the Pembina field is only one of the fields in the area. The Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company also operates a number of fields in my constituency, particularly in the Whitecourt block, so-called, and they have been active recently in developing extraction plants and pipe lines in this area.
There is one other point which should be brought to the attention of the committee. Just recently hearings before the Alberta conservation board were completed with regard

to the application of the Pembina group to do what they want to do with the by-products for all of Alberta. Essentially they have proposed that they will build a pipe line system in Alberta and export up to 75,000 barrels per day of by-products into the Chicago market. These people who have come to us for incorporation under the name of Aurora Pipe Line Company have suggested that they have a market for something like
11.000	barrels per day through their marketing system in the United States. I am one of those who feel that we should try to develop any possible market for our petroleum industry and also for the by-products industry.
Several things were brought out in Pembina's presentation to the Alberta conservation board of which I think the committee should be made aware, and which in my view make it necessary for the house to pass the bill we are now considering. First of all, I should like to refer hon. members to the statement of the hon. member for Bow River with regard to incorporation. I think the principle of the bill is whether or not we are going to allow these people to incorporate. I believe in competition, and I think it is vitally important in this instance. However, in my opinion the bill does bring up a number of problems which we as members of parliament should be considering.
First of all, may I say that we have a tremendous amount of by-products which are going to become available in western Canada, very quickly, particularly in Alberta. I feel that we should be making representations to both levels of government with regard to doing more research into the utilization of these by-products in Canada, and in Alberta or Saskatchewan in particular, or wherever they may be. We should be encouraging the national research council to be doing work on the utilization and the marketing of these extremely valuable by-products.
In the second place, may I say this. This was one of the things on the application of Pembina. When hon. members think that this
75.000	barrels per day is a guaranteed market, they are not correct. This is a question of allowables. I would remind hon. members that a by-product is in essence a competitor with petroleum and therefore will have to be regulated by the conservation board in the same manner as is petroleum; and Pembina, to fulfil their obligations, will require a permit from the Alberta conservation board to delete the 75,000 barrels per day from the other allowables.
There is another matter about which I am particularly concerned, and I should like to say that I have no financial interest in any
Private Bills
pipeline or oil company. However, as a member of parliament representing the constituency of Jasper-Edson I have some concern for the people who are working on this pipe line and for the farmers in my constituency who will want to use some of these by-products locally. I am alarmed by the statement of another Canadian company, namely, Canadian Hydrocarbons, that if Pembina gets what it wants to get, it will be in a monopoly situation and the domestic users in Canada will be hurt by their scheme. These are things which must be given consideration.
There are other means by which some of the by-products will be transported out of the area of production. We have before us another bill to allow the Canadian Pacific Railway to complete an extension into the Rimkey-Home-Glen extraction plant in order to transport these by-products. It is interesting to note that in the recent hearing almost 25 per cent of the producers who were allied with or who had contemplated selling the by-product to the Pembina western oil group, came out against allowing them to do so because they felt that this would put the Pembina group in a monopoly position.
Something has been said by the hon. member for Assiniboia about Texas buccaneers. I want to say to you, Mr. Chairman, that I am not too much concerned about putting any monicker on them. However, we in western Canada are against any kind of buccaneers whether they happen to come from Toronto or from south of the border. I want to say that in my constituency I have a great number of people who have come up from Texas and who are becoming able Canadian citizens. The solution of the question, therefore, is not quite as simple as has been suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South but rather is an extensive proposition relating to an industry which will mean hundreds of millions of dollars a year and thousands of jobs. We therefore cannot just pass it off and say we are going to vote against this bill because of the technicality which the hon. member has brought forward; and that is the only reason that he brought it forward, as far as I can see. I would remind the hon. gentleman that the Pembina group have incorporated Foothills to build a little chunk across the border and the rest of the group will be doing the other part. That course in turn suggests to me that inside the Pembina group there will be little chance for any open tendering or bidding on any of the pipe-line construction which will be done by them.
I should therefore like to leave with the members of the committee what I think are three salient factors in this discussion. First of all, we want to see to it that as much

Private Bills
use as possible is made in Canada of these by-products. We want to make sure that the people who want to use propane, butane, methanol and condensates in Canada have an opportunity to do so on a basis of equality with anybody outside of Canada, if not on a better basis. I would remind my hon. friends that we have a potential market in the grey wood soils in Alberta for a tremendous amount of this sulphur which is going to be produced in this plant in order to upgrade the soils.
In the second place-and I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South in this regard-we must make sure that Canadians are given an opportunity in the development, financing and construction of these lines and facilities. In the third place our policy must be dedicated to the general good not only of Alberta or Saskatchewan but of all Canada. I would remind hon. members that just recently, by resolution, the legislature in the province of Alberta has commended this government for its national oil policy and has upheld it 100 per cent. I do not think that we shall assist by defeating a bill to incorporate a pipe-line company which wants to make application along with several other competitors. It is not only a matter of the Pembina group versus Aurora. Husky, through its affiliated companies, would also like to have a network of pipe lines gathering in the by-product and taking it into the Chicago market. I also understand there are one or two other groups which would also like to do this.
However, as I said before, by defeating this bill we are not going to do anything that is going to help in any way. We have locally the Alberta conservation board which must pass on this application and which must set up the allowables. They report directly to the Alberta government. We have a national energy board which we spent a great deal of time setting up. At the time we did so we as members of parliament said that we are not capable of knowing all of the technical problems which are involved, and therefore we gave to the national energy board the power to sift these applications. We gave them certain criteria by which they were to operate. I am not going to repeat them now because other hon. members have done so, and I am sure the hon. member for Bow River will be able adequately to put them on the record.
I wanted to say these few words because it is most important in my area that some of these things be brought to the attention of the members of the committee. We shall not help the development of my particular part of the country by being restrictive or by trying to keep out United States capital.

We will only help if we go forward and allow these people to incorporate. After that they have to prove their worth; they have to prove they are going to allow Canadian participation in financing construction and everything else.
This is what I think we should do in this regard. We should allow them to go ahead. We want a free country; we want a free industry. We can best develop the resources of western Canada by free, competitive enterprise, as has been clearly shown by the development of Alberta to date as compared with that of the neighbouring province of Saskatchewan.

Mr. Chairman, I know we have all listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks just made by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson. It was a truly magnificent demonstration of how to sit on the fence, present arguments on both sides and deny your own government's philosophical policy on Canadian development. There were quite a number of arguments as to why this bill should be defeated, and then it was sanctimoniously said, "Because of my constituents"-who are not even affected by this bill-"I shall have to vote for it". Then in the last sentence the hon. member referred to Saskatchewan, which is not even concerned in the bill now before the committee.
When this bill was first introduced in the House of Commons I opposed it on principle and on the basis of my understanding. I opposed it in committee. I am opposing it now in this stage of discussion, where we can discuss its principle. I have no hesitation in saying that as long as I am in order, on every stage of this bill as it goes through, I will oppose it. I will oppose it because it is a disgrace to parliament that we, the members of the House of Commons, should be asked to give our stamp of approval to the incorporation of a company which is detrimental to the good of Canada and detrimental to the good of the province of Alberta, as it is.
The only way to discuss and understand the import of this bill is to relate it to the oil industry of Alberta, not particularly as a straight petroleum production but only what this bill deals with; that is, the utilization of the by-products of the petroleum industry. I refer to the methanes, the butanes, the propanes and the condensates, none of which are now utilized in the province of Alberta.
The hon. member for Jasper-Edson, if I heard him correctly-and I think I did-indicated that Aurora Pipe Line Company or its parent company, Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited, will be utilizing some of these things in Alberta. If that is what he

meant, then I say that is the exact opposite of what we were told in the committee by the four representatives of Aurora Pipe Line Company who appeared before us in the railway committee room.
I asked a direct question. It will not be found in the record of the first half of the proceedings of the committee meeting because that portion was not covered by a reporter, but you will find that the question was asked of the four men representing Aurora Pipe Line Company, "Do you intend to utilize, or have you any plans for utilizing the butanes, the methanes, the propanes, the condensates, any one of the by-products, in any existing industry in Alberta, or do you intend to establish any by-product industry in Alberta?" The answer was one word, "No".

Mr. Chairman, may I just inform the hon. member that when I was talking about the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company I mentioned very specifically the fact that they had an interest in what we call the Whitecourt field and that they were, along with other companies, at the moment building extraction plants at Winfield, Whitecourt and Edson in Alberta. The by-products which they are producing there have nothing to do with Aurora at the moment.
This bill concerns Aurora Pipe Line Company.

Yes, but when I was making some general remarks I mentioned that Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company did have interests in other gas fields in the province of Alberta in this particular area. I said that these by-products would be available and are available for Alberta industry and Alberta farmers. That is all I said.

Then if what the hon. member for Jasper-Edson says is correct, this committee is being led astray, the provincial government of Alberta is being led astray and the people who invest money are being led astray. I say this because the hon. member has just said it has nothing whatsoever to do with the bill now before us for incorporation of this company and-
I was talking about the general by-products industry.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
You have had your say; allow me to have mine. At the moment I am concerned with facts.
Oh, oh.

We have before us a bill to incorporate Aurora Pipe Line Company, a subsidiary of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas

Company. Everything that we are being asked to approve in this bill is concerned with the collection and the export, not from Alberta as a whole but only from the cream of the oil area of Alberta, the southwestern area.
I am sorry; my hon. friend shakes his head. He had better not shake it too hard because it is empty and it will fall off. Obviously he does not know what this is all about.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question?

the states of Idaho and Montana. The company is owned 68 per cent in the United States. The hon. member talked sanctimoniously about free enterprise and competition in this connection. This is a company to which we, the members of the House of Commons, gave our stamp of approval two years ago.
May I say I have no interest in Aurora Pipe Lines, nor in the Hudson's Bay Oil Company nor in Continental Oil Company, in Pembina or, indeed, in any other company. I have one interest only, and that is in the Canadian financing, Canadian control and Canadian development of Canadian resources.
That is the way you people opposite used to be, too.

Yes, that is the way hon. members opposite used to be and it is the way they are supposed to be now, the way set out in the speech from the throne. I ask the committee to remember that only two years ago, for the collection and utilization of oil byproducts of Alberta as a whole, for the use of these products in Alberta and in Canada, and for their export only in the case of surplus, we granted the incorporation of the Foothills Pipe Line Company. In case there are Conservative members here who have forgotten, that company is owned 90 per cent by 2,000 Canadian investors, and of those 2,000 Canadian investors 50 per cent are citizens of Alberta. Moreover, 95 per cent of the company's financing-its debt financing-is from Canadian sources.
Is that company talking about a $15,000 short pipe line to be constructed at a total cost of half a million dollars? The answer is, no. Have they been able to get contracts to guarantee the money to finance the Canadian and American project? The answer has been supplied. The answer is, yes. One and a half million dollars-no, not one and a half million dollars-but $130 million. As well, they guarantee priority demand and supply for anything that can be required or developed in secondary industry in Canada as to the use of petroleum by-products, and in addition give an undertaking that only the surplus shall be exported to the Chicago market.
How different this is, reflecting the interest of all Alberta, not a segment of Alberta. The priority goes to Canadian industry first; export comes only second. It is a Canadian owned and controlled company, not an Amerian owned and controlled company. It is a company with $150 million, not one and a half million, and one that has contracts now. My hon. friend over there shakes his head. He cannot figure out why a socialist is speaking this way in a capitalist world. Well, it is because we have to face the realities of this

world we live in, and in the transitional period from the old, decadent system of free enterprise to the new socialist era we shall assist in any way whatsoever where something can be done for the Canadian development and financing of our own Canadian resources.
Amen.

The hon. member does not know the meaning of the word "Amen". He does not even know the meaning of "O Canada" or the Lord's Prayer, because if he did it would be Canada and the people first, always. Just think it over some time. I should like to meet the hon. member on a platform some day on that subject.
We ask the committee to make a ledger and put Aurora on one side, with all that it means, and put the other company and all it means on the other.
There is room in Alberta for them both.
I do not know. I would like to see you and a couple of others try to get into one telephone booth.
They got 17 in one.
It depends on the circumstances and it also depends on the circumference. We are now discussing the development and utilization of the petroleum by-products resources of Alberta.
I am glad you told us.

We say that anyone who is realistic, anyone who does not take a parochial view but a provincial and national view, will have to agree after a study of the facts that the introduction of the bill before us now was an absolute disgrace. It cannot result in a betterment of Canadian interest or in a more efficient development of Canadian resources. Behind it is only one thing, the fact that there is no capital gains tax in Canada, and this is another racketeering manipulation of a stock and corporation for the benefit of individuals; another group of Texas buccaneers who this time are called Continental Oil.
I am amazed that so many hon. members on the other side should have forgotten the words the Prime Minister used when he was on this side of the house in regard to certain oil company transactions. I take great pride in the fact that an hon. member from British Columbia should have risen first this afternoon and, as a Conservative, expose this bill asking that all of us should oppose it, as responsible members, and turn it down. That is the only right, honest and decent thing to do.

I did not intend to speak on this bill, but having listened to the frantic speech of the hon. member for Vancouver East proclaiming Canadian ownership I am tempted to intervene.
Certainly I am in complete support of Canadians having some say in the planning and development of their country, but I certainly welcome additional capital to help in this development and that is what is taking place in the present instance.
Fifteen thousand dollars.

Well, $15,000; but they are still going to provide a market for
11,000	barrels of our product a day. In their speeches on this subject on first and second reading the hon. member for Timiskaming and the hon. member for Vancouver East went on and on talking about the development of secondary industries. I know we must study this export picture because we do not want to export anything which could possibly be used to greater advantage here in Canada.
What is the actual content of it? I asked Mr. Burgis what the makeup of this product is and he replied that 90 per cent was gasoline. Certainly hon. members of this committee will not argue with the fact that there is a surplus of gasoline in Canada. We should try to create for this product as large a market as possible. That is precisely what we are doing through this bill. The hon. member for Vancouver East said that by supporting this $1 million expenditure we would do away with the possible expenditure of $150 million. Nothing could be further from the truth. There is a great demand in regard to the exportation of oil products in Alberta. The Pembina Pipe Line Limited would like to export 75,000 barrels per day. Certainly exporting 11,000 barrels per day would not do away with that proposition on behalf of the Pembina Pipe Line Limited.
What did the socialist party have to say last year when a similar bill was introduced in this house by the hon. member for Kinders-ley, a bill to incorporate the Northern Pipe Line Company which intended to export oil and oil by-products from Saskatchewan? There existed at that time a company exporting oil and oil by-products from Saskatchewan but this was an additional company intending to operate in that province. In a speech made by the hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam he is reported at page 4381 of Hansard for May 31, 1960 as follows:
I should like to hear him, either when he concludes the debate or maybe this information can be made available when the bill is referred to the committee, on the reaction of the government of Saskatchewan in regard to the application for incorporation of this company.

The main concern of these socialists was to find out the opinion in this regard of their socialist friends in Saskatchewan. The hon. member for Kindersley at page 4381 of Hansard of the same date is reported as follows:
I will see that that matter is taken up with the proper parties.
The hon. member for Kindersley is reported earlier in the same paragraph as follows:
I am quite sure my hon. friend agrees with me that the government of the province is most interested in the development of the resources of the province and will do everything it can to co-operate with us in getting this company incorporated-
That was the only concern of the socialists at that time. They would be satisfied if it was satisfactory to those people in Saskatchewan. There was no great expenditure involved. I understand it amounted to some $12 million, but as long as the Saskatchewan government agreed then the hon. members here had no objection.
What do we find in their opinion today? We find that they are trying to make a mountain out of an ant hill. There is a $15,000 expenditure involved but they are trying to blow this up out of proportion and trying to claim that because we are going to grant permission to export 11,000 barrels per day we will disturb the possibility of exporting 75,000 barrels per day. I feel that any suggestion along this line is sheer nonsense.
What did Mr. Burgis say with regard to Canadian participation in this company? He said the board of directors consisted of three Canadian directors, representing Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company; three United States directors, representing the Continental Oil Company; two Canadian directors representing the public shareholders at large, and two senior officers of the company. I would suggest that the Canadians on that board of directors certainly have the right to participate and direct the affairs of the company. Certainly hon. members cannot object to the composition of that board of directors.
Those hon. members who object to the passage of this bill are attempting to create a monopoly as far as I can see. Nothing endangers democracy more than the creation of monopolies. The socialist party would like to create a monopoly and then get into power and take over this monopoly. Perhaps that is the reasoning behind their actions. I fail to understand what their main objection to this bill is except that they are perhaps attempting to raise a political fuss about it. The hon. member for Assiniboia appeared recently on television and said that if the party to which he belonged was in power it would socialize pipe-line companies. He said that

the government under the direction of that party would build its own pipe lines. If he intended to spend $15,000 I would suggest that he would not socialize much of this country.
I would certainly solicit the support of every hon. member in regard to this bill in an attempt to help create greater markets for the oil and gas industry in Canada. I feel there is sufficient gas and oil in Alberta to enable the Pembina Pipe Line Limited as well, as this company to export from Alberta.

The remarks I wish to make are few. Just because the devil is against this particular bill is not sufficient reason for me to support it. I think it is very salutary that this committee should scrutinize very closely any controversial bill coming before it. Some hon. members have said that it is only a bill incorporating a pipe line and it is purely a technical thing. I must say that we are not incorporating a laundry or a peanut stand or anything of that type but a pipe line. I feel that a pipe line or a railway or any public utility is of vital interest to the public and that it is incumbent on hon. members of this parliament to scrutinize the incorporation of any public utility very closely.
I understand that the building of a pipe line involves the powers of expropriation of private property and exploitation of natural resources. These are of extreme interest to the public and should be examined thoroughly at each stage of our proceedings. I say therefore that it is a salutary thing that we scrutinize this bill closely. This parliament or the government must not abdicate its responsibilities in favour of any board or commission even of its own creation. In the final analysis parliament is responsible and must accept that responsibility be it for ill or for the good of the Canadian people.
I have very little knowledge and certainly no interest in the substance of this bill but I think it is very important at this stage, as at every stage, that we scrutinize it. This is a responsibility we cannot abdicate, as I have said. I feel that we must look further into the matter regarding Canadian participation in comparison with other competing pipe lines. I do not think we can dismiss this as a technical matter and depend upon a provincial board or commission in regard to the establishment of a public utility such as a pipe line.

I have heard a few very interesting points raised so far in this debate. One point just made by the hon. member for Stormont had regard to the basis upon which we should look at bills of this nature.

He suggested that we should examine the bill so as to find out if it serves the best public interest.
This is what we in the C.C.F. party have said in regard to this particular bill. We have been accused of having various ideas but those accusations are not true. We are attempting to make sure that this proposal is in the interests of the public. This is what we have been doing at each stage, and what we have been doing through the amendments which we have proposed at the different stages of the consideration of this measure. We have sought to find out whether this particular company if incorporated would in fact serve the best interests of the people of Canada or would in fact serve the interests of some other company in North America to a degree which would be detrimental to Canada. This was the sole basis of our discussion of the bill on second reading and indeed in the standing committee and in this committee also.
Regardless of hon. members on the government side of the house who have objected to this course and who have attempted on a number of occasions to raise points of order that would deter us from this course of action, like the hon. member for Stormont, we feel that we must at all stages closely scrutinize the company, its relations with other companies and with our industry and our economy, not only in Canada as a whole, but in the province of Alberta also, and its relationship with other countries.
In this regard I think we cannot be too careful, nor do I think we should be deterred from that course in quoting extensively from the provisions of the legislation setting up the national energy board. We should not say, as some hon. members from Alberta have said, "Well, after all, the national energy board has been established; it has certain functions to perform and accordingly we think we should give just a quick look at the bill before us and leave everything to the national energy board". We in the C.C.F. of course refuse to go along with the approach that merely because we establish a commission or a board with certain authority we should abdicate all of our responsibility and give to that board or commission the right to do everything.
As I said, I believe there are some hon. members from Alberta who advocate this approach. I do not think it is necessary to mention their names because it is not an issue in this particular instance. All hon. members know to whom I am referring. Their remarks are in Hansard, and in the record of proceedings of the committee, for everyone to read.

We approach this particular bill to incorporate the Aurora Pipe Line Company from this point of view. Will it serve Canadian interests? When I say "Canadian" I mean all of Canada. Will it serve Canadian interests to the fullest possible extent, or is it merely a smokescreen to serve the interests of others who are not Canadians, those for whom the Prime Minister apparently has great affection, contrary to the opinions he held about them a few years ago?
After listening to the two hon. members from Alberta who have spoken today one would think that each of them is putting in his oar for the leadership of the Social Credit party. I refer to their references to the welcoming of capital-
Tim Buck is supporting the hon. member.
My hon. friend knows full well that Tim Buck does not support me.

I know my friend has a one track mind and likes to cast aspersions whenever he gets the opportunity.
The hon. member is doing a very good job.

This is typical of a fascist-minded individual, to grab onto the tar brush and smear everybody and everything when he cannot defend his own position in supporting a certain line of action, Mr. Chairman.
The hon. member has cast aspersions on some other hon. members and now he is objecting when something is said about his party or himself.

I don't live in a glass house.

I am trying my best to proceed in an orderly way but certain things get in the way from time to time. It amazes me but the hon. gentleman, and I am using the singular, appears to have a screw loose in his head; it is the one which controls his tongue. The hon. member for Acadia interjected his comments, and perhaps I should deal with one or two of them. I did not particularly intend to deal with them, but what he said earlier in this debate made me wonder whether he had in fact read the speech from the throne or heard about it, because it was the speech from the throne that contained the reference to Canadian control of corporations. The hon. member is advocating something entirely contrary to that in that he is advocating the establishment of the Aurora Pipe Line Company regardless of Canadian control or of the speech from the throne. Don't put words in my mouth.

It certainly is not.
That is a fact; the hon. member may as well take it.

I did not realize that the hon. gentleman had such an effect upon the government. I did not realize that the government supported this particular bill, but obviously it does and it did not mean what was said in the speech from the throne about Canadian control if we can believe what the hon. member for Acadia says. Obviously, the Minister of Finance did not know what he was talking about in announcing government policy about the Canadian control of industry. We have just had word about the government policy in this regard but apparently it was not correct. I know the Prime Minister says a lot of things from time to time, but I did not realize that he was quite so off base as he apparently is in this regard.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has implied that I said something which I never said. In my speech a few moments ago I read from the committee proceedings the amount of participation that Canadians would have in the direction of this company. There would be three Canadian directors and three United States directors; there would be two Canadian directors at large and two directors at large from the company. Certainly this points

out that Canadians will have good participation, in fact a better participation in this company than their share holdings would warrant. Certainly Canadians will have a fair amount of control of this company.
In my remarks I said that this government and Canadians wanted to have some say in connection with the development of their natural resources, but certainly we welcome financial capital and aid in the development of those resources.
The Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company is 67.8 per cent controlled by Continental Oil Company of the United States of America.

I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has the inside track on those things or whether he is misinterpreting what is contained in the committee's report, but let me read from the Financial Post's survey of industrials for 1960.
