What about the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited which is the company sponsoring the Aurora Pipe Line? It is owned to the extent of 22.6 per cent by the Hudson's Bay Company and 67.8 per cent by the Continental Oil Company of the United States of America. I am reading from the Financial Post's survey of industrials.
If that is not sufficient indication, may I point out that information about the ownership of this particular company was also given by the hon. member for Winnipeg South, the co-sponsor of the bill, and by Senator Thor-valdson who sponsored the bill in the other place. Whom am I to believe? Am I to believe the rash and brash hon. member for Acadia or am I to believe the hon. gentleman who appeared before the committee?

There again, this is in the evidence. If the hon. member did not believe it he should have asked Mr. Burgis to clear it up. The hon. member was at the meeting of the committee and he did not raise the matter at that time. He sat there like a bump on a log. Now he gets up and speaks just to take up the time of the house.

If it is a question of taking up time without contributing anything, obviously we have just had a good exhibition of that. If the hon. member for Acadia wans to engage in side issues of this sort I would ask him to remember that I said initially that it is the approach of the C.C.F.

that we do not want to give up our responsibility and do not think that parliament should give up its responsibility, as the hon. member for Stormont said, to committees or boards or commissions or other bureaucratic organizations that are established. We do not believe in quoting extensively from the acts establishing these boards to show that they have certain powers and then saying that we do not have to do anything except to give the bill a cursory examination and then pass it. That is what the hon. member for Acadia said as found on page 39 of the proceedings of the committee. I will read the whole paragraph so I will not be accused of misquoting. He said:
Mr. Cathers and I agree on a lot of things. I agree with him in his theory-
In his theory.
-that parliament should not pass on to boards anything which would be within the jurisdiction of a member of parliament. I have a gross dislike of how boards have used people at times. In this case, however-
Now he qualifies it.
-a company is here asking to be incorporated. What if the company already was incorporated and wished to export this product? It would not come to parliament at all. It would go to the national energy board. In other words, the national energy board is set up to serve a function. You and I would not have a voice in this if the company had been incorporated already. In other words, a company which already is incorporated and which wished to compete with Pembina could present argument and you would not have an opportunity to say too much about it.
There is this twofold approach again, Mr. Chairman-
I disagree.
-obviously designed to overcome his remark on second reading when he said the same thing only more definitely, that we should give up this responsibility-
I never said anything of the kind.

-that we should not concern ourselves too much with the full effect of the incorporation of this company. His attitude was: Let us not look too carefully into the effect this is going to have. After all, we have the national energy board. Let us just pass the bill without too much argument. Let us not inquire too much into the effect it is going to have. After all, we have got the national energy board, a Tory appointed-

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is again putting words in my mouth in saying that I made this statement for a reason. I presented an argument to the hon. member for York North who had put forward an

argument against the bill and had said that the committee should investigate it fully. I placed a proposition before him. I asked him whether, if the company had already been incorporated, parliament would then investigate the matter and his answer was "no doubt not". I just used an example to try to point out to the hon. member for York North that the national energy board had a purpose and a function. The hon. member for Skeena has gone on to interpret my remarks as meaning something that I certainly never said and certainly never meant to say.

Mr. Chairman, this is not the
first time we have seen hon. members opposite interpret what they said initially and which they wish they had not said in the first place. An example, of course, is the veterans affairs committee where hon. gentlemen opposite practise politics and wish that they were not on the government side. That is just another indication. In any event, I suppose the theory is that if you are on the government side you should not worry too much about anything-
That is absolutely false and you know it.

-or inquire into anything too much. My friend is going to get apoplexy if he is not careful. Even when I am speaking in general terms he seems to think that what I say applies to him. I cannot help that. If the hat fits he will have to pull it right down over his ears and make it quite obvious that he thinks of himself in these terms which I have only used generally.
The hon. member for Jasper-Edson made one reference which I should like to have cleared up, and I am sure he will be able to clear up any misunderstanding on my part in a more gentle way than has been the case in the last few moments. The hon. member for Jasper-Edson referred to Pembina, the other parent company of Foothills, and I understood him to say that Pembina would in fact be a monopoly and that this would be injurious to the people living in the Whitecourt field and that part of the country around Edson and Jasper. I would ask the hon. member to let me complete my statement before he replies. I understood him to say that under Pembina there would be no open bidding on the pipe line itself because it would be a monopoly that would operate to the detriment of all concerned including those who might want to bid on the supplying of pipe, I presume, or on the construction of the line. I understood him to say that there would be this rigid, monopolistic control which would not be advantageous to everyone concerned. I
Private Bills
see that the hon. member is rising and perhaps he may want to clear up that point before I proceed.

I appreciate the opportunity to clear up the hon. member's misunderstanding and I assure him I will do so gently. First of all, I said that the representations before the Alberta conservation board created some doubt and that some of the people opposing Pembina's application felt that if it were granted Pembina in effect would have a monopoly on the by-products industry in Alberta. I mentioned particularly Canadian Hydrocarbons, the local domestic distributors of propane, butane and associated by-products.
I might tell my hon. friend that this has nothing to do with Whitecourt field which is in essence another gas field now being developed and which will be linked up with the export of gas to California. Various byproducts will be available from that field. This has nothing at all to do with Pembina.
What I did say was that there was some fear in Alberta that if Pembina were granted a licence to do what they wanted to do they would be in a monopoly position. It is also a well known fact that Pembina is connected with a pipe line contracting firm. As a matter of fact, their agreement with Standard Oil was filed before the Alberta conservation board and it sets out that Standard will look after the engineering and construction of the pipe line for Pembina. I do not know whether the hon. member is aware of the arrangement that Pembina and Foothills have with Standard of Indiana.

I gather that the hon. member asked me whether I was aware of the arrangement that Pembina had with Standard Oil. That was dealt with rather extensively at another stage. It is interesting that one point has been cleared up by what the hon. member has just said. Notwithstanding all bis earlier remarks about his own constituency, we can see now that Aurora Pipe Line Company has absolutely nothing to do with it and that it is far removed from it. That is the point I wanted to clear up.
We were discussing the by-product situation in Alberta generally.

I want to point out also that, if we are going to draw inferences-and I think we must do so in this instance especially in view of the comments of the other member of the hon. gentleman's party who is rather closely related to him-the inference is that Pembina is by itself of not much value to Alberta because it is a monopoly.

Not at all.

Private Bills
All right. Pembina is not a monopoly or will not be a monopoly.
1 think this matter should be cleared up, Mr. Chairman, because I do not want the hon. gentleman saying things which he knows are false.
Oh, I would not do that.

Not unless you could get away with it. What I said was that evidence was brought before the Alberta conservation board to the effect that if Pembina and associated companies received a permit to do what they wanted to do, they would in fact have a monopoly. I did not say that I said they had a monopoly. I said that qualified people who appeared before the Alberta conservation board had said they might have a monopoly. I would appreciate it if the hon. gentleman would at least stick to a few facts.
I am always interested in facts, but there is no sense in getting excited about the matter.
I am not excited.

The hon. gentleman said, if I have it correctly this time, that apparently qualified experts who appeared before the Alberta natural gas conservation board said that if Pembina gets a licence it will in fact be in a monopoly position.
That is correct.

I do not know whether the hon. gentleman, in making that reference, agrees or disagrees with it. I think we all know that we tend to draw forth factual statements in order to support a particular position of our own. I hope the hon. gentleman does not agree-he may do so; I do not know- but I should like to know whether he agrees or disagrees with the comments of those qualified experts, namely that Pembina will be in a monopoly position.
This is an extremely important matter, Mr. Chairman. I do not want any member in the opposition to misunderstand my position. I tried to clear up this matter on second reading and I tried to make it quite clear in my opening remarks today. My position and that of the C.C.F. with regard to this matter is not one of Pembina versus Aurora or Foothills versus Aurora or whatever the name might be. It is a matter of which is going to be to the greatest advantage of Canadians and of Albertans; in this instance, their interest is one and the same. I want to have that point particularly clear because I do not want hon. gentlemen opposite later on to be going out and accusing me of supporting a monopolist corporate structure. That is why I want to

get this particular point clear. But if it has been made clear that the hon. member for Jasper-Edson is not in fact himself saying that Pembina will be a monopoly or in a monopoly position-
Of course I am not saying that.
-but is only saying what others have said-
That is right.

-then we have that point cleared up; and I hope that later on no one- because he may say that I opposed Pembina or opposed Aurora-will make the accusation that I was in fact supporting a monopoly. I want to get that point clear-
Oh, oh.

-because there are other people, like the one who has again broken the rules by speaking from his seat, who may make these accusations and cast reflections on what people do at every turn of events, every time they get the opportunity to do so; and even when they do not get the opportunity, they are prone to do this.
In any event the point of view from which we must approach this matter is this: Is it or is it not beneficial to Canada, compared with other circumstances, to have this particular company doing the things it seeks to do under the corporate powers which it seeks and with the financial structure it seeks to have? Moreover, is there something additional that it seeks to do or that it might do with these corporate powers and with this financial structure? This matter we can deal with a little bit later.
At this time I should like to say this. I do not see the hon. member for Vancouver South in the chamber at the moment. He may be unavoidably absent. However, I should like to say that the hon. member for Vancouver South in his initial comments did a decent analytical job on this Aurora matter and outlined his position quite clearly. When this bill was before the house for second reading it will be recalled that those of us who wanted to find the full implications of it were told that we would get the full story and the full picture in the standing committee. We were told that one of the reasons why standing committees existed in so far as private bills were concerned was that people would have an opportunity of appearing and of presenting their case, and that committee members would have an opportunity of querying them about all and sundry matters in which they might be interested.

In this particular instance-whether by coincidence or by design, I do not know- it was unfortunate that one of the major organizations, or rather the other major corporate organization concerned about the particular bill was not able to be there. We know they appeared before the committee of the other place, although that committee kept no record. We almost kept no record either, not having done so until we were part way through. In any event we know that Aurora and Foothills appeared before the committee of the other place and I think every hon. member of the house expected that they would also appear before our committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines which considered this particular bill. Unfortunately, they did not do so. This failure to appear left a fairly large gap in the evidence which was presented.
As the hon. member for Vancouver South said, it is not always so much what is said in a committeee that matters but rather what is not said. I am quite sure that the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas people who were there were presenting information-I do not say they were hiding anything-and arguments which would support their particular application and that they would not in fact present arguments which would support Pembina's stand if it was opposed to them. This is a natural course for people to follow. However, we reached the committee and we did not get the information in full or complete form.
Perhaps this is a good time at which to mention that possibly what we need on these committees or attached to them is a staff of research people who will be able to go into these subjects and advise members of the full impact of things so that all members of the committee and of the house will have a better opportunity of assessing the effect of them. However, perhaps this is not the point at which to deal with that matter.
In the committee the hon. member for Westmorland attempted to do what I think was the decent thing to do. It is unfortunate that it was not carried out. As found at page 46 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee-and this was fairly well at the completion of the evidence of the Hudson's Bay Oil people-he moved as follows, and I quote his words so that I will not be accused of paraphrasing them. He said:
But, I move that before going on with the clause by clause discussion, that the meeting be adjourned to a later date in order that anybody who might oppose the bill will have an opportunity to give evidence before the committee.
Then he went on further to state as follows:
However, I think it is our duty to give the public ample opportunity to get here, and for that
Private Bills
reason I am going to move that this committee hearing be adjourned for a period of one week before we take it clause by clause.
I think this was the decent and correct thing to do, especially in view of the earlier evidence which was given by the hon. member for York North. I make reference to him only in the sense that he appeared and gave evidence. It is quite true that he mentioned the fact that he had a particular axe to grind in that he was a shareholder in the other company which had opposed this Aurora Pipe Line Company bill before the committee of the other place. I will quote what the hon. member for York North said as reported at page 37 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee. This was after we finally got shorthand reporters there. The hon. gentleman was not reported in his initial evidence. In any event, he did say:
It is in answer, I think, to a remark by Mr. Winch about how this was advertised. I would like to add that the Pembina people had intended to be here, but the hearing is going on today in Calgary before the conservation board, so they could not be here.
I subsequently asked him whether they desired to appear, and so on. He claimed that he would not know because he appeared, as I understood it, not as an agent or representative of Pembina but as an individual shareholder. In fact, when he finished his evidence I think he said something to the effect that perhaps Pembina would rather he had not come.
However, the hon. member did point out at the committee meeting on Tuesday, February 21, 1961, that the Pembina people had on that day intended to be here but they were before the Alberta oil and gas conservation board. That was extremely unfortunate.
Following upon that the hon. member for Westmorland moved that the meeting be postponed for one week. There was then some argument as to whether or not the meeting was adequately advertised. Reference was made to the fact that advertisements had been placed in the Canada Gazette and the newspapers. Undoubtedly there was advertising in connection with the formal notice of petition for a private bill, without reference to the actual date of the meetings of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
I should point out in this regard that it would be pretty difficult for those advertisements to have contained the actual date of the meeting of the committee.

speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired. Shall clause 1 carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure that the hon. member for Skeena would

Private Bills
like to continue. I will just say a few words and then he can carry on. I think we were indeed fortunate in this house, and in the committee, to have people on the committee who were not concerned with hearing only one side of the matter. We were indeed fortunate to have on the committee such people as the hon. members for Vancouver South, Vancouver East and Skeena. These members were interested in seeing that both sides of the story were presented.

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? Does he know how great a part the hon. member for Skeena took in the committee? Does he know how many questions the hon. member for Skeena asked in the committee? Has he read the committee proceedings?
I will tell you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member for Skeena is quite capable of telling you himself how many words he spoke in the committee, if that is what you want to know. However, although I am not a member of the committee, I did sit in on the committee meeting and listened to the discussion. I think these three hon. members put forward a fairly comprehensive argument in support of the contention that the application of Aurora Pipe Line Company was not all that it seemed to be, nor was it all that the sponsor of the bill indicated.
I am suggesting that hon. members of this committee who did not have the opportunity to sit in on that committee, and who have not taken the opportunity of reading the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee, would have been quite impressed with the presentation made on behalf of the opposition which should, in my opinion, have had an opportunity of being there.
In this regard I should also point out that the hon. member for York North brought quite a number of points to the attention of the committee that would not otherwise have come up. I think the members of this committee and those who are interested in pipe lines being built by Canadians for the distribution of Canadian products for the benefit of Canadians would have been quite impressed by the presentation that was made on their behalf.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps it may be an interesting sort of diversion if I counted the words I used in the committee, as required by the hon. member for Acadia; but I do not intend to do that. He knows the answer to that question as well as I.
I think that on the question of personal participation as between himself and myself

in the committee, he was perhaps more verbose than I. There is no doubt about that. This applies in the house also.
However, I was dealing with this matter and I should like to continue. I had raised the matter as to whether or not there was a full opportunity for interested parties, particularly Pembina, to attend this committee meeting. That day they were unfortunately before the Alberta oil and gas conservation board. Because they were unable to attend that committee meeting, I wonder whether they should not now be given the opportunity of appearing. This could be done by the committee undertaking-perhaps we should do this in a formal way later on, Mr. Chairman; I merely toss out the idea as a suggestion-to rise and report progress and recommending that the bill be referred back to the committee. In that way interested people who were prevented from appearing earlier could now appear.
There was some argument about this. Pembina were obviously the major corporate organization that was interested; they appeared before the committee of the other place which dealt with this particular bill. The hon. member for York North, who appeared as a witness, stated that Pembina intended to be in Ottawa, but unfortunately they had to appear before the Alberta oil and gas conservation board on that day. There was quite a discussion in the committee about advertisements. It was said that even though there was no date in the advertisements pointing out when this committee of the house would be meeting, nevertheless anybody who wanted to find that out could do so.
This is quite true. Anybody who wanted to find out when the committee was meeting could do so. I do not wish to quote the words of the hon. member for Acadia, who told somebody else that he had no vital interest in it and then mentioned to my hon. friend for Vancouver East that he could have found out and that other people could have found out, but the words are there. It is a fact that if something is to be presented before a committee of this house, and it is set down for hearing, anyone who is interested can in fact find out when that committee will meet. It is published in the Journals, a letter to a member of parliament will obtain this information, or it can be obtained by a communication to the clerk of the committee. There are a number of ways of discovering when a committee is going to meet.
However, the fact of the matter is that on February 13 this year this bill passed second reading in the house. After extensive debate, on February 13 it passed second reading and was referred to the standing committee. One

week later, on February 21, the committee met to consider the bill. There was only one week between the time the bill was read a second time and its perusal by the committee.
The Pembina people, who had a vital interest in this matter, who the hon. member for York North said were going to appear and who had appeared before the committee of the other place, could not be here on February 21. Why could they not be here? It was because they were appearing before the Alberta oil and gas conservation board. They obviously could not be in two places at once.
Even if the Pembina interests had known-[DOT] and I am not saying that they did not know -that February 21 was the day set for the hearing, do you think they could have prevailed upon the Alberta oil and gas conservation board to postpone its hearings so that they could come to Ottawa? I think not. The Alberta oil and gas conservation board undoubtedly has a number of people appearing before it in connection with applications for licences. Undoubtedly they have a number of hearings and have to set a schedule and keep to it as much as possible.
The decent thing would have been to follow the suggestion made by the hon. member for Westmorland and postpone the actual clause by clause consideration of the bill for one week in order that interested people could be there, and specifically in order that one interested group of people-and I am not advocating their case at the moment; I am merely pointing out that they were an interested group, Pembina and the Foothills company-could be present. It would have been proper to postpone the clause by clause consideration for one week in order that the Pembina people could have come forward to present their point of view, put forward their ideas and participate in eliciting information from the Aurora people, and vice versa, in order that some of the unanswered questions which are still in the minds of hon. members might be answered so that at this stage the committee of the whole considering this bill might have a more complete picture than the one-sided picture we have at the moment.
I do not wish to cast any reflection on the action taken by the committee, because that action has now been taken, but I think it was regrettable that this course should have been followed when postponement of the discussion for one week could have meant all the difference in the world. As I suggested before, I do think this committee of the whole might reasonably express the view that an opportunity should be given to the Pembina people to appear and present their point of view. I do not know whether this should be done in any formal way at the moment. In
Private Bills
fact, I do not know even if it would be in order to move the particular motion which I have in mind.
Perhaps before any action of this kind is taken, the sponsor of the bill who has worked hard and assiduously to promote its passage through the house might care to comment on this suggestion that the committee of the whole might report its considerations to the house, one of those considerations and recommendations being that the bill be referred back to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines in order that it might go more fully into these particular questions.
I know one could level the accusation that this is a delaying tactic and that anything which consumes time is a means of delay, but in this particular instance I submit that would be an incorrect conclusion to reach, because one of the things I am concerned with is the right of people to present their views and their ideas. The Pembina people were denied that right. There is no question about that. Of course, they could have appeared before the committee on the day which had been advertised, had they known about it, and thereby foregone their right to appear before the Alberta oil and gas conservation board, but they could not have been in two places at once. In the circumstances the proceedings before the Alberta board were, perhaps, more important for that company since they involved licensing. In any event, the company chose to put forward their case before the Alberta board on the same day as our committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines was meeting.
It seems to me that this committee might profitably follow the course I have suggested, bearing in mind that we are not attempting to postpone things or to call things off but merely trying to give these interested people an opportunity to appear before a standing committee of this house, an opportunity which was previously denied them because of circumstances over which, I am sure, they have no control. Action along the lines I am suggesting would preserve the undeniable right of individuals to appear before a standing committee and present their views on particular questions, whether in opposition to them or in favour of them is immaterial to me, the major principle involved being the right to appear. I think this committee will agree that by force of circumstances, if for no other reason, the Pembina people did not have the right to appear before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines on February 21.
Possibly, following such an appearance we would be in a position where the doubts which have been felt by some hon. members here would have vanished to the point

Private Bills
at which they are no longer doubts at all. The suspicions which some hon. members may have with regard to the Aurora Company might be seen to be without foundation and it might appear to be in the best interests of Canada and Alberta for Aurora Pipe Lines to proceed. At the moment, however, when we have been presented with a one-sided picture, one party-an interested party-having been unable to appear before a committee of this house, I think the only decent and correct thing we can do is to provide that such an opportunity be given. Perhaps at another stage, later on, after we have had some discussion on this point, it may be logical to move a motion to that effect, but before we actually reach the formal stage of doing so we may, perhaps, have the opportunity of hearing the comments of one or two other members and learn whether or not they think it would be the correct thing to do.

In view of the fact that there have been some allegations that proceedings of the committee of which I am chairman were not carried out in a proper and orderly manner, particularly in connection with the fact that a certain body was not allowed an opportunity to appear before the committee, perhaps I might briefly intervene at this stage.
The hon. member for Skeena made reference to the fact that the committee hearing was advertised in many newspapers. Advertisements giving notice of the meeting to discuss the matter of a private bill for incorporating a company known as Aurora Pipe Lines appeared in at least 12 and, possibly, 15 papers in September of last year. The company concerned had a perfect right to petition the committee and ask for the privilege of appearing before it at any time but we did not get an application of that type from the Pembina people or from the other pipe line company affected.
In fact, knowing the opinions of the hon. member for York North, a member of our committee, on the very day when this bill was passed on second reading and referred to the committee I asked the hon. member for York North if he would like to have his people appear in opposition to the proposal before the committee. They were notified, at that time, when the committee meeting was to be held but after that there was no indication from the Pembina people that they wished to offer any opposition to the bill. Therefore, I maintain that at no time were they denied the right to appear. They had a perfect right to appear before the committee and we could have changed the date of the sitting if they had indicated they wished to

come. No indication was given that they were going to be in attendance and we did not think it was necessary to postpone the meeting. The meeting was then called for February 23.

I have just one comment to make, Mr. Chairman, in regard to the remarks made by the hon. member for Welling-ton-Huron who was the chairman of that committee. I understand he just referred to February 23 but I did not catch what he said following that reference.
I was referring to the date set for that meeting. Perhaps it was February 21, 1961.

I take it the hon. member was referring to February 21, 1961 the date the committee was to have heard the witnesses representing this company.
I was referring to the advertisements that were made in regard to the petition for incorporation, as the hon. chairman of that committee said, sometime last September. These advertisements did not, in fact, mention that the committee was to sit on February 21, 1961 to consider this particular bill. As I understand it there was no advertisement to that effect. Perhaps my understanding in this regard can be cleared up. Were there any advertisements in regard to February 21 being the day upon which the meeting would sit for the purpose of considering this bill?
The hon. member should realize that committee meetings are not advertised in newspapers. These meetings are advertised in the Votes and Proceedings of this house.

Yes, I understand that was the only method of advertising. I wanted to make sure that was clear.
As I have said, there was a considerable amount of discussion regarding newspaper advertisements. I think the hon. member for the Yukon mentioned that he had seen an advertisement in the Whitehorse Star. I am sure that this was widely advertised, as is required by the rules of the other place.
Unfortunately I was not quite able to hear what the hon. member for Wellington-Huron said in regard to the hon. member for York North being in touch with the Pembina people respecting the proposed hearing date. Would the hon. member indicate what he said regarding the hon. member for York North?

I did not indicate what the hon. member for York North had said. I did indicate the proposed date and time of the meeting and suggested that he might get in touch with the Pembina people in this regard. He intended to inform me as to their wishes in respect of appearing before that committee. If

these people wished to appear before the committee it was indicated that a day would be set to correspond with their wishes.

These difficulties have probably risen through unfortunate circumstances.
At page 37 of the minutes of proceedings of that committee, I asked the chairman a question which is reported as follows:

Because of his close association with Pembina perhaps I might ask Mr. Cathers whether they would desire to appear before the committee following the hearings in Alberta before the oil and gas conservation board.

I would not know.
I took this to mean that the chairman did not know if the hon. member for York North had received an indication that the Pembina people wished to attend or did not wish to attend. I want to have this situation clear. In view of the fact that the hon. member for York North is, I gather, our only contact in a formal or informal way with the Pembina people, I would like to know whether or not he intended to convey the impression that they wanted to appear or did not want to appear. I feel that perhaps in view of the fact that he is only a shareholder and not an official acting on behalf of the company we should perhaps refer this back to the committee in order to find out whether or not these people, who perhaps through unfortunate circumstances, were not in a position to participate in the hearings, wish to appear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have enjoyed listening to the debate which has taken place this afternoon, and it seems to me a fundamental difference in opinion has been revealed. Perhaps this is one of the occasions when the members having this difference of opinion should refrain from taking part in the debate.
The difficulty involved in regard to a pipe line operation is the fact that it is transmitting a natural resource from one place to another. In this case it is seeking to transmit condensates which are very similar to crude oil. We are faced at this time with the fact that one company has already been giving fairly extensive coverage across the provinces in the distribution of oil and oil products. I am referring to the Pembina Pipe Line Limited, whose officers appeared before us a couple of years ago. They were given at that time what has amounted to almost a monopoly. I would suggest that we look into this situation and find out if this monopoly is in the public interest at this time.
In handling any natural resource a transportation factor is involved, because of the necessity of providing highways, railroads and pipe lines, some of which are built at the public's expense. I think that this is
Private Bills
perhaps an argument in favour of putting railway services under a public utility monopoly. I feel that each time we deal with natural resources or the transmission of them we should take a look at the distribution history of other natural resources. I believe that if we did so we could only come to the conclusion, as many people did in 1957, that the transmission of natural resources should be controlled by a public utility board.
There does exist in Canada today one pipe line company distributing oil and oil products from the western provinces and it seemed to me at the time this company was incorporated that it would eventually expand perhaps to the extent that it could look after the market developing in the Chicago area. Anyone belonging to the C.C.F. party believes that there should be exportation of natural resources. It seems to me, however, that this company is only interested in the exploitation of natural resources, particularly oil and oil products, through the transmission of these products, using a branch line running into the Chicago area and that there would be very limited expenditure necessary. It seems to me this company is interested in the exploitation of the oil industry through milking off very rich profits from a very short distribution line which will send the product to a trunk line running into the Chicago area where a very limited amount of expenditure will be necessary.
We have heard conflicting stories about $15,000 being enough to make the connecting link across the international border. If this is true, if the Canadian people are going eventually to fit their export market into this kind of action, then it would have been a very nice thing, in my opinion, if we had built this line as a public enterprise and as a public utility. If we had built this $15,000 link across the international border we would have had complete control of distribution into the export market.
Those who talk about exploitation should bear in mind that they are federal members; that they represent not only a small oil area of Alberta but all of Canada. They are not elected here as the representatives of a particular area but as members for all of Canada. This point has been argued by prominent parliamentarians down through the years and I do not intend to duplicate the argument at all. It is an established fact that members represent not only a very limited area or a limited interest but the country as a whole.
Bills of this kind have to be sponsored. There is no kick against anybody sponsoring these bills. According to parliamentary procedure they have to be sponsored by somebody. It may be quite an honour and

Private Bills
an opportunity to sponsor a private bill, I do not know. I hope it never falls to my lot to sponsor one in which I am vitally interested or concerned because I think it would be very difficult to remain impartial and still be closely connected with the particular industry concerned.
In this committee there are a number of hon. members from Alberta who are vitally concerned with the production of oil and the sale of oil, and particularly with the money which will result from and flow back into their own areas because of the sale and export of oil. I have no kick against that, Mr. Chairman. Probably they are doing their duty to their constituents; that is what they should be doing. But there is a great deal to be said on behalf of all the other people in Canada.
I have been interested in the stories we hear about our having too much oil. It is said that we have too much gas and too much of everything. In northern Ontario we pay over 49 cents for a gallon of ordinary grade gasoline, and we pay 51.9 cents for grade one gasoline. It would appear to me that there probably is quite a spread between the cost of the production of the gas that is exported across the border into the Chicago area and the gas that reaches me in northern Ontario. I looked up the Canadian Statistical Review, which is probably a pretty shoddy way of finding out how much petroleum products is exported and how much is imported because it is not broken down in a way which would give you that information. If we were more closely conversant with the various factors in those condensates we would probably come up with a little more accurate figure. The committee was told that in its natural form these products are made up of about six parts condensates, one part butane and one part propane, and when they are processed through the plants the various condensates end up as four parts condensates, one part butane and one part propane. We were also told that they were a very high type product; they are the basis for high grade gasolines and oils; they are a competitive product with crude oil that is being imported into the country.
It was interesting, in looking at this copy of the Canadian Statistical Review, dated January, 1961, to find out that with respect to petroleum products, in 1958 we exported $6.4 million worth; in 1959 we exported $6.7 million worth, but at the same time we imported $6.5 million worth in 1958; and $6.5 million worth in 1959, of the same petroleum products. This would indicate to me that there is a large market in Canada for these products. If we are importing petroleum
[Mr. Peters.l
products to this extent, then there is an opportunity for processing some of these products into gasoline and oil, and that is what I am particularly concerned about.
Northern Ontario is completely a natural resources area. It has no major secondary industry development; it has had very little in the way of transportation. We are not blessed with any large bodies of water or other natural geographic features to enable us to be anything other than a natural resources storehouse, and this area has produced very little industry over the years other than industries based on the natural resources. In this respect, our resources are phenomenal and have contributed to the development of such cities as Toronto, but we get very little benefit from the production of our natural resources. In the very early days perhaps there was some justification for the buccaneers coming in and exploiting our natural resources.
People from the Ottawa valley have come into our area and cut down the trees. They have floated them down the waterways and taken them out of the area completely. It is advantageous for some to say, "Let us take the condensates out of the area; we have no plants that will manufacture them". A secondary industry development is necessary to put these petroleum products on the market in a form in which they can be used. We in northern Ontario have not this development. I for one would not like to see other areas develop where exploiters would come in and exploit the area. We should do everything we can to see secondary industry developed as close as possible to the source of the natural resource.
If it is necessary to spend $15,000 to build this pipe line, then goodness gracious, surely the Canadian people could afford to do this, if it would give them the key to the complete control of the Alberta oil fields and the export markets. If this is the gateway into the export market, then let us get control of this and export only what we cannot develop for ourselves.
I think we should learn a lesson from other areas. Let us look at northern Quebec where we have a fabulous iron industry, as we have a fabulous oil industry in Alberta. This country is not getting much advantage out of the iron industry in northern Quebec. It is true that a few miners are employed, and the few people who are connected with the development that takes place in this type of industry. If we had kept the gateway of Seven Islands we would have the largest steel mills in the world situated in that area. I think the same is true with respect to these condensates, if we took control of them. If

they are as important as they appear to be, let us keep them in Canada and develop them as far as we can in Canada. Let us sell the finished product to the United States public who will be demanding it as they are demanding other natural resources. I think it is this simple.
In recent months I have been impressed with some of the statements that have come from the Conservative hierarchy in which they have said, "Let us put some control on the exploitation that is taking place by the use of United States capital. Let us retain some of these advantages for the benefit of the Canadian people." This matter has not only been discussed. A few controls were instituted not long ago with regard to the establishment of companies and that may be in part the reason why Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company did not itself ask for a charter that would have extended its rights and allowed it to construct this pipe line. These controls may have had some effect and it may be of interest to some of the financial geniuses to sit down and figure out how much less money will be derived from taxation because of the establishment of this new company than would have been the case if the development had been carried out by the parent company or one of the other companies participating in this development along with the parent company.
In my opinion these are all problems that cannot be dealt with by the national energy board. It has been said that the national energy board is going to make the final decision on a number of these matters. That is true but it cannot make any decision on where we put secondary industry in Canada. If we have secondary industry the board can only decide that a certain amount of the product must be available to Canadian plants and for Canadian development. If we are to do our duty in parliament we must put some roadblocks in the way of those from outside this country who would exploit us so that we will be able to develop our own products. I think the national energy board then has all the authority it needs to see that industry we establish on the Canadian side of the border will be able to function to some advantage.
We have heard a great number of charges levelled today about whether there was a proper hearing when the bill was considered by the standing committee. I was surprised at the vote that took place in that committee. I am not disclosing anything that is not known. I was not a member of that committee and the fact is reported in the procedings of the committee. I was interested to see that again in my opinion party lines were drawn so as to forestall a number of members who

wished to have a delay which would have allowed the chairman of the committee an opportunity to ascertain whether the opposition, the Pembina group, was interested in appearing before the committee and opposing the bill.
I think this is again an example of one of the great failings in the functioning of committees of the House of Commons. We do not have any source of making information available to people who might be involved and in many cases we do not know who is involved. I think many members of the standing committee were surprised when they found a member of their own party standing up in that committee-
Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I should like to suggest that the hon. member for Edmonton West jumped to a conclusion with regard to what I was saying. I did not intend to mention how anybody voted. AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before the recess hour, Mr. Chairman, we were trying to point out that this type of application has implications that are far-reaching, that there is a difference of opinion and that the difference of opinion is rather a fundamental one. We are trying to make our position clear. Our position is that this is a large natural resource that is being tapped; that although this company has made application for a small and inconsiderable program, it comes to parliament and asks for wide powers for a large corporation and that this can be a large and influential segment of our economy as it affects the oil industry.

A great deal of responsibility has been left with the national energy board. I think most of us can and do agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East when he pointed out that in setting up this particular company you are setting up a new type of distribution that is going to have only as the basis of its initial program the distribution of oil not through Canada but into the export market of the United States.
Some of the hon. members who have participated in this debate have pointed out the Canadian content in this particular company and how it is comprised. I believe that we have an obligation, particularly in view of the many statements that have been made from the Conservative party and the C.C.F. party. I believe that, from the C.C.F. point of view, consideration should and must be given to using our national resources for the advantage of all Canadians and that, from the Conservative party's point of view, greater consideration should be given to Canadian control and Canadian ownership. In both these respects this company fails to meet the requirements.
We have been told that the national energy board will protect both these interests, that all we have to do is to pass this bill and we shall have accomplished only the setting up of a company or a corporate body, and that then the national energy board and the conservation board of the province of Alberta will make the decision as to whether it is in the interests of the Canadian economy or of the Canadian people and as to the extent of the export licence that this company will be given. I think it is interesting to note however, what has been said about the application of the energy board act to this particular company. The sponsor of the bill, as reported at pages 37 and 38 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee, quotes part of the National Energy Board Act, refers to Section 27 and states as follows:
Section 27 says:
Except as otherwise provided in this act, a company shall not begin the construction of a section or part of a pipe line until
(a)	the board has by the issue of a certificate granted the company leave to construct the line.
In this respect we have been told what has been done by this company which just does not exist in fact, although the sponsor of the bill talked about the flexibility of the law, the flexibility of legal arguments and certain other flexibilities. This company does not and will not exist until this bill is passed. Yet they have already gone to one of the boards, namely the board in Alberta and have asked for certain considerations. However, actually in fact there is no such company.
In that respect it is just like the new party.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There may be some similarity; I do not know.
I hope not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is the analogy that both of them are meeting with stiff competition before they are born. There may be some similarity in that respect. Then he goes on to show what is necessary; and I am quoting from the statement of the sponsor of the bill:
Section 44 sets out the kind of evidence which shall go before the board:
The board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, issue a certificate in respect of a pipe line or an international power line if the board is satisfied that the line is and will be required by the present and future public convenience and necessity, and, in considering an application for a certificate, the board shall take into account all such matters as to it appear to be relevant, and without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the board may have regard to the following:
(a)	the availability of oil or gas to the pipe line, or power to the international power line, as the case may be;
(b)	the existence of markets, actual or potential;
(c)	the economic feasibility of the pipe line or international power line.
On those three points, when and if this bill is passed and if this company is formed, the board is going to have a great deal of difficulty in assessing even the limited information that is now before the committee. We have by law set up one organization in this field of public utility. We have set up an organization which came before us and asked for a distribution and collection system of pipe lines that fairly well covered the whole area and which at that time indicated that it could more than meet the supply that was available at the time. Now we are increasing the decision that will have to be made by the board because we are saying to the energy board, in effect, that we feel that one company was not able to meet one of the requirements and that the second company was needed. We are also deciding that we are having to have a second company because of the existence of markets either actual or potential. If we have not filled the markets which the original company agreed to fill, I would think that we are giving to the national energy board a direction to the effect that here is another company that must be given part of the potential that may arise in the future.
As to the economic feasibility of the pipe line, if it is only a matter of $15,000, I think even the Canadian government could afford at this time to build that small section of the pipe line. I therefore assume that with a large company having the opportunity and 90205-6-171

the resources of revenue that they obviously have and the money that is available for pipe lines, there is not much question that they will be given the opportunity under this section to produce the line. The sponsor of the bill then goes on to say this:
And this is one of the points you raised.
(d)	the financial responsibility and financial structure of the applicant, the methods of financing the line and the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line;-
Under section (e) parliament stated, when setting up the national energy board, that it would have the right to choose as follows:
(e)	any public interest that in the board's opinion may be affected by the granting or the refusing of the application.
I would assume that the national energy board would take into consideration the fact that we have decided there should be a second company competing with the first one in this particular field. They would have no alternative but to say, "If the government is going to give them a licence to set up a new company, we are going to have to give them a licence to allow them to make some use of this particular company".
Are you advocating a change in the powers of the national energy board?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not think we ever intended to give the national energy board the right to say what was in the interests of the Canadian people from one period of time to another. I should think that when the legislation was passed setting up the national energy board the Conservative party was not on this anti-American kick that they are on now. Times change and direction changes. I assume that parliament itself is the body that should decide what is to be accomplished, and it should not be left to a board to make that decision.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, the hon. member is imputing that the Conservative party has certain underlying motives with respect to the oil and gas industry in western Canada.
This is a bill to incorporate a company. We have a national energy board. As far as we on this side are concerned, we have every confidence that the national energy board will take care of the various problems referred to it in the best interests of all Canadians. I very much resent the implication of the hon. member with respect to what this government may have in mind.
Is this a speech or a point of order?

It is a point of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I believe parliament should be supreme in deciding what the position is going to be in relation to the wishes of the Canadian people. We, as the representatives of the people, should interpret the wishes of the people and make changes if necessary. But a board is not in a position to make these changes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.
Mr. Chairman, we are taking this opportunity to make our views known-
Very interesting.
As always.

-on this bill. We are doing our part to point out the weaknesses in the legislation before the committee, the reason why this bill should not be passed and the fact that the government in recent years has completely changed its attitude to legislation of this kind.
I think the bill now before the committee should not be here at all. When we were discussing the bill on second reading some of us pointed out what we thought to be very great weaknesses in it. We were told by some hon. members opposite that the bill was merely to set up a corporate entity, that it had nothing to do with policy and that it was merely for the establishment of a company that, under certain other laws and regulations, would appear before the national energy board.
We were also told that second reading of the bill was not the stage at which to obtain detailed information about the company. We were told that the proper place for this to be done was in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines where all information would be made available, where witnesses would be called, where hon. members would be given every opportunity to inquire into the bill, to obtain particulars of the proposed company to be incorporated and, in general, to satisfy themselves that this legislation was in the interests of the people of this country.
That committee met. Very little evidence was adduced and very little opportunity was given to hon. members to find out the details of the measure involved or to find out to their satisfaction whether this legislation should be passed. But there was some information obtained in the committee, and if there had been any doubt about United States control before the committee met, there was certainly no doubt after the evidence of Mr. K. H. Burgis, the vice president of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company.

Mr. Burgis had this to say in his opening remarks:
The application for incorporation of Aurora Pipe Line Company is being sponsored by Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited. Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited was incorporated under the laws of Canada in 1926 and its shares are listed on the Toronto stock exchange. Approximately 10 per cent of its outstanding shares are owned by some 12,000 public shareholders, 22 per cent by the Hudson's Bay Company and 68 per cent by Continental Oil Company.
Therefore, the fact is on record that we are dealing with a company which is largely United States-owned and which is and will be largely United States controlled. Hon. members opposite are saying to us that this is not government policy, the government has not given its stamp of approval to this legislation. I suggest that the government has approved of this legislation. I suggest that the government clearly demonstrated that it is 100 per cent behind the legislation, in that when the vote was taken on second reading the cabinet lined up solidly in support of this measure.
This is a rather startling disclosure in light of the stand taken by the Conservative party when in opposition. Not only did the Conservative party in opposition oppose United States control of companies like this one, but when the Conservative party was in opposition it opposed measures which had to do with this very company in question and went on record in opposing this kind of United States control.
Nonsense.
That is not nonsense at all; that is a fact.
A fact to you is not a fact to anybody else.

The Conservative party has had many leaders in the past; they change quite regularly. In 1956, when they had one of the temporary leaders of that party, the Hon. George Drew, he had this to say, as reported at page 2177 of Hansard:
The present distribution of the ownership of this enterprise shows also that the control is in the hands of financial interests in the United States; that it is definitely under the control of these immensely powerful financial interests: Canadian Gulf, Hudson Bay Oil and Gas and Tennessee Gas Transmission,-
These were the all-powerful United States companies that were so opposed by the Hon. George Drew in his day but which are taken to the bosom of the Conservative party in power. This company is given the blessing of the government and the great battle put up by Mr. Drew in former years has gone by the board. This government, in practice and

in office, has disowned and disclaimed everything that he said in relation to United States control of gas pipe lines.
The Hon. George Drew went on to say this in regard to the same question:
Contrary to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, this is the occasion to focus attention on our resources. This is the only place to do so and this is the opportunity to declare our economic independence of the United States.
That was the song in opposition. The theme in government is, ostensibly, the same but actions speak louder than words and the party in power is now prepared to turn over this pipe line monopoly to a United States company.
Would the hon. member permit a question? I wonder if he would mind reading the rest of Mr. Burgis' evidence at page 35 of the proceedings in so far as voting rights are concerned.

If I may conclude my sentence, I should be very glad to comply with the request which has been made. I was saying that the government in power is now turning over this monopoly to a group of United States interests controlled by the Texas buccaneers to which the government made such grave objections in days gone by.
Now I am asked to read from Mr. Burgis' evidence following the quotation I have made. This is from Mr. Burgis:
Despite the disparity in shareholdings of Hudson's Bay Company and Continental Oil Company, each have by agreement equal voting rights and equal representation on the board of directors. The present board of directors consists of three Canadian directors representing the Hudson's Bay Company, three American directors representing Continental Oil Company, two Canadian directors representing the public shareholders and two senior officers of the company.
Having regard to the distribution of the shares and the measures for the control of the company as they have been set forth, there is no doubt that this company will be United States controlled as well as United States owned.
I had expected that this committee in dealing with this legislation would have held a great many hearings and would have called to appear before it a great many witnesses so that all the details of such an important bill might be inquired into. Unfortunately this is not what occurred. Those of us who are not members of the committee learned this afternoon that the proceedings of the committee during a substantial part of the time were not recorded and transcribed, with the result that the evidence as far as we are concerned is just hearsay evidence. No record was kept, and the hon. members on that committee did not take action soon 90205-6-1714

enough to have that evidence taken down in order that members of the house might have the advantage of the record before them. This certainly makes a mockery of the statement made on second reading that the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines would provide an opportunity to bring forth evidence so that hon. members on all sides of the house might be able to peruse it and learn all the details about the company which was to be incorporated. I am flabbergasted that the committee has been so slipshod in its proceedings, or that the committee should have been so disinterested-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sure the hon. member realizes that he is criticizing the proceedings of the committee. That is contrary to our rules.

I think I went a little far under the rules when I said they had taken a slipshod attitude. That expression might be a good one for horse dealers but it is not good as far as a committee of the house is concerned. I will say, then, that apparently this committee did not consider this legislation of sufficient importance to think it worth while having all the evidence transcribed. I would say that the committee failed to perform its functions in such a way as would be most helpful-perhaps that might be in order, Mr. Chairman-to hon. members of the house. It is one thing to be able to go over evidence that is available; it is quite another to have evidence given of which no record at all has been kept.
I do not understand why the committee was not prepared to call additional witnesses. I do not understand why the committee was in such a terrible rush to get this legislation back to the house unless, perchance, it was because if it were sent back soon, or immediately, the legislation would not be dealt with at very great length and thus, in the opinion of the sponsor, have a much greater chance of being passed during the current session.
None of us, I am sure, is happy or would prefer to use private members' days to discuss private bills at very great length but we are not masters of the rules. The rules are as they exist in the various editions of Beauchesne and we must govern ourselves accordingly. So we have the opportunity during this whole day to discuss this bill and its provisions and the very great lack of evidence of a worth while nature which has come from the committee to this chamber. We all know that this company is not designed to do something which could not have been done if the company had not been brought into existence. We

Private Bills
are all aware that there is another company involved in the same field-the Pembina company.
Are you in favour of the other company?
I am not in favour of one company as against the other.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Gladly.

I want to ask one cardinal question. Is the hon. member in favour of marketing this tremendous resource of the province of Alberta provided only that no expense to the federal treasury is incurred, or does he wish to retain it for posterity?

That is a very pertinent question and it was put very directly by an hon. member who is probably the most persistent questioner in the house. Certainly he runs interference with most members who are speaking.
The answer is simple. We are in favour of marketing all the surplus of Canada's natural resources on a planned basis in such a way that will bring the greatest benefit for this and future generations. We are not only in favour of marketing those resources now, where there are surpluses, and net surpluses; we are in favour of getting the greatest possible return for the Canadian people and we are interested in marketing those resources in such a way as to avoid selling out our country to United States interests and United States pipe line companies. We are no more interested in 1961 in selling our country to these pipe line operators than were the Conservatives when they were in opposition in 1956. The main difference is that the Tories have changed their policy and we have insisted on maintaining ours.
Is the hon. member suggesting that by passing this bill we are indeed sanctioning the marketing of these resources?

Mr. Chairman, when the government majority, sometime during this session, pushes this legislation through the house I suggest that they will be taking a course that is not the most preferred one, a course that is not necessary, and one which will in fact be insulting to parliament and to the Canadian nation.
Would the hon. member make a comment as to the national energy board in that same regard?

Mr. Chairman, the national energy board is apparently bailing out the

Tory party from all the mistakes it is making in regard to this particular measure. I do not think the responsibilities of the members of parliament can be foisted on the national energy board. I am speaking of the responsibilities of the members of parliament to examine bills coming before this house, and the responsibility to decide whether or not a given company should be incorporated. After we have made that decision the national energy board will make its own subsequent decision.
I suggest that this measure before the committee should not be passed. I suggest that it be turned down in the interests of Canadians. I suggest that there are alternative means by which the fuel products involved can be marketed and we can do more in the interests of Canadians by turning down this bill at this time than we shall do by passing it.
Mr. Chairman, the bill was before the committee and was apparently given some consideration. I am unaware of any presentation urging amendments to this proposed legislation. I am not aware of any amendment at all being suggested by the committee. I would suggest that the committee gave, in a very hurried manner, a rubber stamping to this legislation, and hurried it back to the house but failed to bring forward the kind of information that was in order.
On a point of order. When the hon. member refers to the committee rubber stamping the desire of the government he certainly is not in accordance with the practices of parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have warned the hon. gentleman that he should not speak disrespectfully of any decision made by the committee or the members thereof. I would ask him again to be more careful in his wording.

Perhaps I should not use the words "rubber stamping". I should use the words that were used so often by the Hon. George Drew, "trained seals". There is considerable evidence that they did not need the party line laid down for them by the whip in the house, they were able to gather from the united stand of the cabinet which way the party winds were blowing, and the bill had no difficulty whatsoever in the committee.

I rise on a question of personal privilege. The hon. gentleman is calling me a trained seal. I am not a trained seal. I am just as independent in my thinking as is any member of the hon. member's party. I am interested in developing western Canada's oil and gas industries. I am trying

to approach this problem very dispassionately and will not accept the hon. member's suggestion that my thinking is done for me by someone else.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a comment. The hon. member for Medicine Hat very strenuously objects to being called a trained seal. I apologize. He is an untrained seal who is learning very quickly. I think if he is here much longer he will be a trained seal, and will be just as efficient as the hon. members of the previous administration who were accused so often by the Hon. George Drew of being trained seals.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would suggest that the hon. member in correcting his first remark has made it worse and would warn him to be more careful. If I understood him correctly in his first remark he referred to a group generally. I did not think he was referring to the members of the committee. If he did so this would be too specific a remark. In apologizing to the hon. member for Medicine Hat I feel he has gone too far and would suggest that an appropriate rectification is in order.

Mr. Chairman, I think that I was in error if I applied this terminology to the members of the committee because it has much broader application. When any of the hon. members who have spoken today say that this is a government-sponsored bill I want to assure them that in sponsoring this bill I am doing so as an individual member of parliament.
It seems to me that the criticism of this bill boils down to two points. I should like to answer both of these points individually. If I understand my good friends who have spoken against the bill, it seems to me they are opposed to it because they find that there are United States interests behind the company which is asking for the incorporation of the company in question. Second, if I understand their arguments aright, they are against the export of the by-products of natural gas from Alberta.
Let me deal with the first point first, and I do so sincerely. I appeal to hon. members. I emphasize that we are merely asking for the incorporation of a company. Whether hon. members like it or not, in 1959, when the National Energy Board Act came before the house, hon. members supported it. I should like briefly to review the sections of the act which they supported. Whether they like it or not, or whether they stand in their places tonight and say that we are going to hand over this particular jurisdiction, the facts are that, according to the National Energy Board Act, they did in fact and in law hand over that particular jurisdiction to the national energy board.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Now we are taking it back.

I do not want to get into an argument; it my hon. friends will hear me out, they have asked for some information and they will get that information. I want to go back to my original argument before there was a digression and deal particularly with three sections of the National Energy Board Act, namely sections 10, 27 and 44. As I said before, when I spoke on second reading of this bill, section 10 of the National Energy Board Act sets out that the board is a court of record. As I said on that occasion, a court of record hears evidence either by documents, verbal evidence or any other kind of evidence, and from that evidence it makes certain decisions. What is the decision that the national energy board makes? It makes this decision. It decides whether the company can have a certificate to build a pipe line, whether a half mile, 41 miles or how many miles it is. That is the specific function of the national energy board as set out in the National Energy Board Act which all hon. members, I believe-and if I am wrong I wish somebody would correct me-supported in this House of Commons in 1959.
What does section 27 say, Mr. Chairman? Section 27 says that provided the evidence is satisfactory-and I am not going to go into what kind of evidence is necessary-then a certificate can be granted to build a pipe line. If there are four or five applicants certain considerations arise and I want to come to that point in a few moments.
We have heard a lot about Foothills Pipe Line Company-this seems to be the darling of the C.C.F. or of somebody-and they come before the national energy board and they set out the facts. They say that 95 per cent, if that is the correct figure, is capitalized by Canadians. Our company has set out the facts honestly and fairly-I do not think anyone can deny that-that 68 per cent of the stock of the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited will be owned by Continental Oil Company of the United States of America and 22 per cent by Hudson's Bay Company and 10 per cent by the public at large. These are the facts taken into consideration. If these facts meet the standard set by the national energy board whose chairman is Mr. McKinnon, who was for years chairman of

the Alberta conservation board, then someone, a pipe line company, will get a certificate to build a pipe line. That is the first point.

Those are the functions of the national energy board which was established by the members of this house, and all supported, the board's creation and jurisdiction. When they supported it they created a court of record to consider these things in a technical manner, in a manner in which all the evidence and all the pros and cons are weighed. If the national energy board considers that one company has more Canadian financing that is one of the ingredients that will be taken into account. In fact, it is not one of the ingredients that may be taken into account. Using "may" in the sense of "shall", the act says it is one of the ingredients that shall be taken into consideration.
Let us get down to the facts of the line itself. It is true that it is half a mile of line. No one in their right sense would suggest tonight that they would commence to build the line first before this company was incorporated and until their application had been approved by the national energy board to build the half mile of line joining the Canadian line across the boundary with the United States line.

For years the province of Alberta has been bulging with natural gas. In fact, the Borden commission found that there are 23 trillion, and some odd billion cubic feet of natural gas as a proven reserve in Alberta. As a by-product of natural gas there is condensate.
