What is condensate? I do not know whether there was a reporter present in the standing

committee at the time this was said. However, it was set out there that condensate is really crude petroleum. If ever a westerner stands indicted in his place tonight, it is with reference to any statement about keeping our crude petroleum within our borders in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Let us look at that matter for a few moments. Condensate will make one and a half times the gasoline that people use for their cars. We are only producing 50 per cent of our capacity in the petroleum industry today in the province of Alberta. We want to produce 100 per cent under the proper rules of conservation which we have.
I cannot believe that these people can be serious in wanting to keep 50 per cent of our petroleum production at home. Let me draw this analysis. Would you keep 50 per cent of your wheat at home in the bins when you can sell it or 50 per cent of your cattle in the foothills when you can sell them? Here is a by-product that we can sell, crude petroleum. Ever since I have been a member of the house we have been wanting to export crude petroleum to the United States. I have not been a member as long as the hon. member for Assiniboia. Experience is a wonderful thing and we can all gain it but some take longer than others and my hon. friend is no exception.
To come back to my point, we have been wanting to export crude petroleum to the northwest states in the United States. That is the very foundation of the national petroleum policy that was announced. If we cannot raise the market volume up to 600,000 or 800,000 barrels per day we are in trouble in our petroleum industry in western Canada. We are only asking that the condensate, which is really just plain ordinary crude, be exported across the line to the United States where it can be used in Montana and Oklahoma.
The hon. member for Vancouver East said that this was not fair to the province of Alberta. Let him go through the province of Alberta and talk to the residents of that province. They will decide what is fair for the province. They want to sell what they produce, whether it is wheat, cattle or petroleum.
I submit in all seriousness and in all sincerity that the thing that would be fair to Alberta is to export the commodities we have so that we can build up our trade and give full employment to our people in that province which enjoys fuller employment than any other province.

Here, on the one occasion perhaps-and this is for the benefit of those who have made this accusation, untrue as it is-when I got to a committee to listen attentively to all the proceedings and to absorb as much as I can, the hon. member for Acadia jumps up and says I should have made just as big a fool of myself there as he is doing here. I can appreciate how he in particular,

and others, can get off on this wrong track. When it is not possible to justify a position, wild statements are made in this house.
I have only one further comment in connection with the remarks made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont. The hon. member referred to the inconsistencies apparent in the committee today.
Be careful now.

I would say to my hon. friend that I am always careful, especially when I am speaking through you, Mr. Chairman, to such an astute and capable member. However, I would point out that the fact is that the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont belongs to a party that is consistent; it is consistently in favour of the Texas buccaneers, pirates, and so on, whom they favoured when they were in power.
I should like to make a comment or two about some of the things which the hon. member for Bow River so flamboyantly poured into this committee a while ago. The hon. member began by saying that he was going to provide us with some factual information. He wound up by saying that he was back where he started from. In the whole process he did not go anywhere. But he did make one very interesting comment. He used one very interesting-I wonder whether it is revealing-phrase when he was talking about the Foothills company, I believe it was, which would go before the national energy board, would have to prove certain things and produce certain information, and so on. Then he said, "Likewise our company", referring to Aurora Pipe Line Company, the company with which we are presently concerned. I think it is important that he should qualify what he means by "our company". Does he mean a company with which he is associated, if he is associated with it? Does he mean the company which is silently endorsed by the government? This is important because it could have a bearing on the voting of the hon. member on a previous occasion. If the hon. member meant by the phrase "our company" the Aurora Company or the Hudson's Oil Company, a company with which he is associated through share capital, then he should not have voted previously on this bill. This is one matter into which we should inquire immediately before we proceed any further. I think that possibly this was only a slip of the tongue and the hon. member is associated with this company simply by being the promoter of the bill.

I appreciate the hon. member having brought this to my attention. If I did use the phrase "our company" I did

so as the sponsor of this measure only. I can assure the hon. member that I have no financial interest as far as this company is concerned and I certainly was not speaking for the government. I made that clear, and I think the hon. member knew exactly what I meant, too. But if he wishes me to clarify my statements I am always happy to do so because hon. members in that comer of the house are always so exact.

The hon. member is jumping to conclusions if he imagines people can always understand what he means. The word "our" is capable of various interpretations but, as I said, it could have been a slip of the tongue.
I should like to point out one other thing to the hon. member for Bow River. The hon. member made reference to the national energy board as a great protective agency. He told us how it kept the interests of the Canadian people always in mind and implied that all we had to do was to follow his ideas blindly and say: this is a good company, and the energy board would then carry out whatever it has to carry out in the best interest of Canadians and everybody else.
The hon. member made reference to the National Energy Board Act, sections 10, 24 and 44. He referred also to those sections in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. In fact he quoted from them and read them into the record. There is an interesting part of this operation which was conveniently glossed over, but it is contained here in the act and it is, I think, worthy of consideration when people talk so much about the national energy board being paramount in these matters.
We are told that this agency is one which works independently in the best interests of Canada-that it is an entity to which certain authority has been given, that there is no interference with those powers, and so on. But what does section 44 say? I recall some objections being raised about this in committee of the whole when the national energy board bill was before parliament.
I am reading now from the evidence at page 38 and I am assuming that the hon. member for Bow River, when he read this, read correctly from the act. I am quoting now from his own statement of what the act contains. If I am wrong, I am sure the hon. member for Bow River will correct me, admitting at the same time, that the error was originally his. I read:
Section 44 sets out the kind of evidence which shall go before the board.
The board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, issue a certificate in respect of a pipe line or an international power line if the board is satisfied-
Private Bills
And so on. So it is not the board which acts as the final agent in protecting the interests of Canada as we have been led to believe or misled into believing; it is the governor in council, or, in other words, the cabinet, which decides.
The board is not, in fact, an agent free of political interference. What could be easier than for this cabinet, this government, to have given its blessing already to the Aurora Pipe Line Company or Continental Oil or whoever their friends are in the United States oil industry, knowing full well it would have to appear before the board at which time the cabinet would approve the granting of permission to build a pipe line? All this talk about the board being an agency to protect the people of Canada is so much nonsense. It is the governor in council who is going to make the decisions, and I think that should be understood.
The hon. member for Bow River was generous in his accusations against the hon. member for Assiniboia. I see they are sitting close together now.
Don't blame me for that.
I know the hon. member for Assiniboia has aspirations to sit on those benches. Perhaps that is why the hon. member for Bow River is there too. In trying to seek out-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

In any event, the hon. member for Bow River did level in a generous way these accusations against the hon. member for Assiniboia. He accused the hon. member of not knowing what he was talking about. Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver South started all this. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Vancouver South, a member of the hon. gentleman's own party, was the first speaker today. It was he who said that Aurora Pipe Line Company had already let a contract for the half mile of pipe line. That contract was let to a firm named R. H. Fulton of Texas. This was the comment as I took it down while the hon. member for Vancouver South was speaking.

I know the hon. member would not wish to be wrong about this but what I understood the hon. member for Vancouver South to say was that the contract had been let with reference to the 41-mile pipe line. In fact the hon. member had mentioned that to me outside the committee.

The hon. member is not a cabinet minister. He cannot speak from there.

Private Bills
A few moments of glory.

I jotted down the words of the hon. member for Vancouver South and I took them to apply to Aurora Pipe Line. My note says that with regard to the half mile section to be built by that company a contract had been let to the R. H. Fulton Company, a Texas firm. It is true the hon. member did at the same time make reference to the 41-mile section and the two sentences were close together. It could have been he was referring to that. This is the question to which I think the hon. member for Bow River should have addressed himself instead of going off at a tangent and accusing the hon. member for Assiniboia of making incorrect statements.
The hon. member for Bow River was the one who left the impression a few days ago that the Pembina people had withdrawn their application to the Alberta gas and oil conservation board. The hon. member for Bow River left the impression by way of a question and because he left this impression by way of asking a question it was impossible for us to deal with it. We have since found that this was not a true impression. The hon. member for Bow River who sponsored this bill did not know what he was talking about in respect of at least one of these companies and for him, of all people, to accuse the hon. member for Assiniboia of making incorrect statements, particularly when that hon. member was basing his statement on the information given to this house by the hon. member for Vancouver South, is certainly very improper.
I suggest it is improper for the hon. member for Bow River to follow this procedure in presenting a bill to this house. It is also improper for that hon. member to level accusations against the members of this party in saying that we are supporting the Foothills company in favour of the Aurora company. It was made clear from the beginning that that suggestion was not to be read into our remarks. We are concerned, as I have said before, with that which is in the best interests of Canada, the oil industry and the general economy of the nation. We are concerned in regard to the rights of interested people and, in this instance, I am referring to the Pembina company.
It certainly was not in the best interests of that company when it was denied the right to appear before the committee of this house on February 21, 1961 when this matter was partially dealt with, even though this may have resulted from unfortunate circumstances. That is the type of thing we are concerned with. We do not feel it is simply a question of whether it is a good thing or a bad thing.

We have grave doubts and misgivings in regard to the Aurora company and the manner in which it has dealt with certain questions.
Certainly there are grave doubts raised by a letter dated January 10, 1961 appearing as appendix A to the minutes of proceedings of the standing committee. This letter was addressed to my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East and signed by Mr. James A. Scott, president of the Pembina Pipe Line Limited. The letter consists of two printed pages. I would like to read a portion to this committee so that all hon. members will be familiar with the situation outlined therein. I feel that I am entitled to read these portions because reference has been made to the Pembina pipe line company this afternoon and the request which was made regarding their appearance before this standing committee. I will read the last paragraph rather than just the sentences of importance so as to present the complete context. The last paragraph reads as follows:
Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited (Continental Oil Company) is now trying to compete with Pembina by offering to take the surplus gas by-product liquids-
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order-
You cannot rise on a point of order, you are in the wrong seat.
We are now in committee, and hon. members can speak from any seat.

The hon. member for Skeena is confused as to the oil company. It is my impression that we are discussing the Aurora pipe line bill and I am wondering why we are now considering Pembina Pipe Line Limited.

Mr. Chairman, I agree that perhaps the discussion regarding the Pembina company is not relevant but this subject was raised in the first instance by the hon. member for Vancouver South. It has been referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver East as well as by myself on earlier occasions. There has been ample reference to this company and I feel, Mr. Chairman, that if you enforce the rules strictly it would be unfair because we would then be left with an impression which is coloured or flavoured but not necessarily accurate. I would not be allowed to contradict those statements and we would be left with an improper comparison.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I feel that the contention made by the hon. member for Skeena is an accurate one. I do not intend to ask him to refrain from discussing this particular matter but I must say that I feel the debate has

strayed from that which normally takes place in the consideration of a clause in a bill. 1 would say that almost every hon. member who has spoken in regard to this bill has been guilty of straying from the subject matter.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to go into this at great length but I would like to refer to the last paragraph because it bears relation to the company which the bill is designed to incorporate.
The last paragraph reads as follows:
Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited (Continental Oil Company) is now trying to compete with Pembina by offering to take the surplus gas by-products liquids from the extreme south of the province of Alberta into the Continental facilities in the United States. They state that they have no present intention of extending the Alberta facilities to handle production from gas fields to the north. If this is taken at face value, Hudson's Bay is prepared to skim off the easy cream of the product at the expense of the other production in the province. Further, such action if permitted might well imperil our comprehensive and equitable system because of the lack of an economic pipe line volume. If it is the Hudson's Bay ulterior intention eventually to extend north into the province, they intend to duplicate what we have been proposing for many months. It is for such a purpose that Hudson's Bay are endeavouring to incorporate a special act pipe line company comparable to our Foothills company.
I have read the entire paragraph so that the important sentences will appear in their context and hon. members will appreciate how they fit into the paragraph as a whole. The main two or three sentences read as follows:
They state that they have no present intention of extending the Alberta facilities to handle production from gas fields to the north. If this is taken at face value. Hudson's Bay is prepared to skim off the easy cream of the product at the expense of the other production in the province.
I assume that this statement means that, if this is a correct assessment of the intention of the Aurora pipe line company, it would be detrimental to the interests of Alberta. That is at least the point of view which is put forward by the Pembina company in this letter. They suggest that if the Aurora company is going to channel the condensates south into the United States without going north they will in fact be skimming off the easy cream of the product at the expense of the other production in the province. If this is a factual statement I would suggest that the whole situation should be explored further. I do not know whether this is a true statement. I know that it appears in this letter dated January 10, 1961 written by Mr. James Scott, the president of Pembina Pipe Line Limited. If it is the intention of the Aurora company to skim off the cream at the expense of the other production then this
Private Bills
will not be beneficial to either the companies concerned, the citizens of Alberta or the citizens of Canada generally.
I think this situation should be clarified. I feel that the officers of the Pembina company should be requested to appear before a standing committee of this house and explain their reasons for arriving at the conclusion as set out in this letter. The Aurora people being there would be able to say, "Well, this is not correct, and this is how we disprove it", because, as I said before, the main concern is what is most beneficial to Canadians and Albertans and to our economy. This is the thing that we want to do. These are some of the questions that still have not been answered. It is quite true that questions of sorts were posed to one of the gentlemen from Aurora in the committee and he said, no, that is not so; it will not be skimming the cream off the crop. I cannot offhand find the particular reference in order to quote it verbatim, but I do recall that it was dealt with to a slight degree.
There is another matter of concern in so far as Aurora is concerned, and it has to do with their future intentions, and whether or not they do intend to proceed further northward into Alberta and perhaps even further north than that. Mr. Burgis of the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited did give some evidence to this effect, which appears at page 48 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee where, in answer to a question posed to him about what else they had in mind besides this little $15,000 line, said:
At the moment, sir, we have nothing else specifically in mind. However, we are, as are many of the other oil companies, in the pipe line business. Frequently, when we consider moving crude or condensate from one field or one market to another it might involve consideration of crossing interprovincial boundaries and at that time we conceivably could use Aurora to build more facilities, let us say, from the Yukon or Northwest Territories into Alberta or something like that. But specifically we have nothing in mind at the moment. We put that in, as most companies do, when they are setting up a corporation which is going to have an indefinite life, to make it more flexible and to have more flexibility to cover future things that might happen.
In so far as it is possible for this gentleman to see into the future, I suppose this does to a degree endorse what Mr. Scott of Pembina said when he took them at their face value in saying that they have no present intention of extending the Alberta facilities for the production of gas and oil into the north. Mr. Burgis said in effect that for the present that is quite true, although at some time in the future they might very well want to go up there. In fact, he did mention that in answer to a question of the hon. member for the Yukon who asked about the authority

Private Bills
and powers to start pipe lines in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
The hon. member for the Yukon asked about activities in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and Mr. Burgis said:
I will be glad to answer that. We have undertaken a fairly extensive exploratory program in the Yukon and Northwest Territories which we hope will be successful in finding oil and eventually might need to build a pipe line or assist in building a pipe line to get the oil out to market. We certainly do not need it yet. We have undertaken a fairly extensive exploratory program in that area.
The witness went on further to say that they had exploration permits there, and that they were active in their search for oil and gas in both the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. I think this goes to prove the comments of Mr. Scott of the Pembina Pipe Line who assessed it in this way, namely that there was a lack of intention on the part of Aurora to extend north into Alberta. Perhaps he was correct in taking it at its face value. In two specific places before the committee Mr. Burgis mentioned that they had nothing specific in mind except building this half mile pipe line across the border into Montana and that, as far they could see, they had no intention at present of going north into Alberta to tap other lines or of going into the Northwest Territories.
I think we must take that at its face value and that it is not the intention of Aurora to go north. If that is so, then I think we should query the conclusion and I think the Pembina people can also, when they say that by so confining themselves to this section of the province they are not skimming off the easy cream at the expense of other production. Apart from the slight reference made to this in the committee, I do not know whether it is so or not, but from the very brief reference in the discussion that was held-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in listening to the remarks of the sponsor of this bill who outlined in glowing and evangelistic terms the righteousness of his company and the relationship that they have and the wonderful job they would be doing for all of the people, particularly of Alberta. It seems to me there is a touch of selfishness developing in some of the hon. members. It seems to me that instead of our friends supporting the buccaneers who were mentioned in the house three or four years ago, perhaps we should start protecting the buccaneers from Texas and from some of the

other places because some of this selfishness would appear to me to be not in their favour.
Here we have a little itsy bitsy company which, according to the sponsor of the bill, should not make any difference at all. He sounded like one of those great Social Crediters who go around with the bible under one arm and with the other hand picking the pockets of the people through exploitation.
It seems to me that we have been told by the sponsor we have this little itsy bitsy company which has only 1 million common shares at $1 a share and 60,000 preferred shares at $50 a share, making a capitalization of $10 million, to build this little itsy bitsy pipe line of one half mile. No matter how the argument goes, I think the sponsor will agree that the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company has already decided that it is going to build the 41 miles. The sponsor is quite right in making the statement that Aurora has not let this contract. I do not imagine they will ever let it. At the present time they have provision for spending only $15,000, and they are going to build just one half mile of pipe line, which is the key half mile crossing the international boundary.
Do hon. members not think that we are pretty naive if we expect this company to go into the United States where they intend to raise $10 million to capitalize a company which is going to spend only $15,000?
Will the hon. member permit a question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member would not allow one but I will.
We are democratic.

We know that. When Foothills Pipe Line was incorporated in 1959 by chapter 64 of the statutes the capital stock of the company was to consist of 10 million shares at a par value of $5 per share, and if they built the pipe line in question it would cost $160,000. What is the difference between Aurora pipe line and the Foothills pipe line in question? It is a matter of form and the hon. member knows it. It is all set out that way in the incorporation of the company.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If we make a mistake once we do not have to do it again. We do not make the situation any better by making the same mistake again. I am not sure that we made a mistake.

Did you vote for it? Did
you support Foothills? I thought you did.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I cannot remember if I was here that day.
The hon. member's memory is bad.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I know I have shown some consideration for western members when they have been interested in the building of pipe lines. I was quite impressed with the attitude of the Conservatives two or three years ago when they wanted to build pipe lines in Canada. I am not so impressed with some Conservatives when they get up and want to build another pipe line before the first one has had a chance to operate. I am not so impressed when they want to build another pipe line for the specific purpose of not allowing any of the product of the first line to bring benefit but rather of taking all the product and shoving it through a second pipe line into the United States.
You don't know what you are talking about. You have absolutely no knowledge of the situation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am not alone in that. I have heard these flexible legal interpretations made. I have heard the sponsor of the bill tell us tonight how he wanted to put the facts on the record. I also heard him stand up and interject not long ago at which time he certainly did not state the facts because he told us the application for another pipe line had been withdrawn and therefore there was no reason-

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, that question was raised in the committee. If the hon. member will read Hansard he will see that I asked a question and I said it was alleged from the knowledge I had that a certain application had been withdrawn. When that question was asked in the committee it was said under oath that the application was withdrawn. He should read the sworn statement and stay with it instead of running away from the facts in the manner he has been.

If I may speak to the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out what the hon. member for Bow River did in the house, and the hon. member for Timis-kaming is quite correct in this regard. The hon. member for Bow River interrupted in the house to ask a question. He did not ask a question but made the bald-faced statement that it was his understanding that Pembina had withdrawn their application.
That is not true.

This was on the very day that Pembina was supposed to appear before the Alberta board. In the standing committee I asked a question as to what had happened with regard to this application and whether
Private Bills
it had been withdrawn. As found on page 42 of the proceedings of the committee there is the following:

Within the last week or two
Pembina and the people-your associated companies-appeared before the Alberta board?
Yes.
They did not withdraw their application?

No, sir. They withdrew only their application to duplicate the portion that we have indicated in green.
That is entirely different from what the hon. member for Bow River led this house to believe-I am speaking to the point of order-not by way of an explanation or formal speech but by way of a back door question. He introduced this information in that way at that time obviously in an attempt to lead those who were speaking then into believing there was no point in inquiring any further into the matter because the Foothills company had withdrawn their application. That was not true. It was only true in respect of that section that was outlined in green. We have not got the map here to show hon. members but that was the situation.

I think I should put what I said on the record. As found on page 1815 of Hansard I said:
May I ask a question at this stage? These are the facts, though I have not yet had an opportunity to substantiate them-the information was communicated to me by telephone.
I set that out and the hon. member who has just spoken has not set out the facts. I continued:
In all probability the oil companies of which the hon. member speaks have withdrawn their applications in respect of this particular project before the Alberta conservation board.
Under oath before the committee it was stated that this particular application had been withdrawn. I do not see how the hon. member can stand in his place and say anything different. I went on to say:
I wonder whether the hon. member has given any consideration to that?
Those are the facts and the hon. member knows those are the facts. If he wants to make statements that are not in accordance with the record, as he has done all afternoon, that is his privilege. The record will speak for itself and the people will know what the record says.
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that both the hon. member and myself are now stating facts.
I will take my facts.

However, I doubt very much whether he can recognize them.

Business of the House

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have been stating what happened and as I was not a member of the committee I suggest now that the hon. member has put forward exactly the same facts from the letter that he read tonight as he put forward the other evening and that they are probably no more reliable tonight than when he got them over the telephone the last time because I imagine they come from the same place. I am surprised he has not got a more coherent story to tell the committee as a result of the many communications he has had with the same source of information. It seems to me that the situation is still very confused as far as the sponsor is concerned. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

No, it is not ten
o'clock.

Order. The hon. member will be happy to learn that it is now ten o'clock.
Progress reported.
I wonder whether I could ask the house leader to indicate the business for the next three days, if he is in a position to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
For tomorrow and Wednesday, Mr. Speaker, there are six items of legislation that we would like to see considered by the house. The first one is No. 11 on today's order paper, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance dealing with the Tariff Board Act. The second item is No. 1 on today's order paper, second reading of Bill No. C-47. The third item is No. 5 on today's order paper, second reading of Bill No. S-5. The fourth item is No. 6 on today's order paper, second reading of Bill No. S-6. The latter two will be referred to a committee. These four items stand in that order for tomorrow.
The other items I have in mind are the second reading of Bill C-71, an act respecting the civil service of Canada, and the second reading of Bill No. C-73, an act to amend the Income Tax Act. I am not certain tonight whether they will be taken in that order. If there is a change I will inform hon. members on the other side of the house before 2.30 tomorrow afternoon.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
